- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 319 file-side / run 324): `arxiv-2611.22515` — Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability (Kenton White — AC Online, Algonquin College; arXiv:2611.22515v1 [cs.LG, cs.AI], 2026-11-17, Accepted at IEEE SSCI 2027, 7 pages, 43 KB source, replication code released). Full text via PDF extraction (~41K chars: abstract, §§I–VII, references). **Substance:** FLEX fits **one** Fisher linear discriminant to a black box's binary prediction matrix. Per label, positive and negative predicted-group centroids give the right-hand side; **one** within-class covariance is pooled over every label's positive group, ridge-regularised at the median diagonal floored at 1e-6, and a single batched Cholesky solve yields all label weight vectors at once. A feature enters a label's list only if a two-sample F-test between that label's predicted-positive and predicted-negative groups survives Bonferroni correction within the label (α = 0.05); the sign sorts it into a positive or a negative list. Two diagnostics follow: the weight-vector norm bounds separability (Theorem 1: two-sided bound by the Whitened centroid gap scaled by the extreme eigenvalues of the regularised pooled covariance, hence a cross-label proxy up to the square root of its condition number), and concentration (largest weight over mean weight) is a black-box signal that the label rests on one dominant feature. Six classical classifiers (BR-LR, BR-RF, BR-XGB, ECC, ML-kNN k = 10, RAkELo) on five Madjarov benchmarks (Yeast, Emotions, Scene, Genbase, Enron; 6–53 labels, 1.07–4.24 labels per instance), 50/50 iterative-stratification splits, ten seeds, explainer given only the feature matrix and the predictions. **Results:** surrogate AUC ≥ 0.90 in all 30 cells and > 0.96 in 25 (lowest ML-kNN 0.901 and BR-XGB 0.911 on Yeast); recall ≥ 0.77, = 1.00 on Genbase; precision from 0.876 (BR-LR Yeast) to 0.245 on Genbase; shared covariance beats per-label AUC in 4 of 5 datasets, by **+0.180** on Enron where per-label condition number is 6.32e7 against 3.44e2 and each label has on average 64 positives in 1,001 dimensions; Genbase reverses (0.999 per-label vs 0.980 shared) at condition numbers 3.54e7 vs 5.72e6; budget sweep monotone for FLEX (best AUC of any method at full budget on 0.964/0.969/0.984/0.995) while trees peak and decay (0.858→0.764 Emotions, 0.828→0.741 Yeast) and Genbase's tree is already 0.993 at one feature; concentration correlates negatively with cross-classifier explanation disagreement on all five datasets, significant only on Enron (ρ = −0.568, p = 0.001) and Genbase (−0.545, p = 0.029), against mean pairwise prediction discrepancy of only 0.4–10.7%, i.e. the classifiers agree on which instances to label and diverge in how.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 324): **A surrogate's fidelity and a surrogate's scope are separate claims, and the tell that a paper conflates them is a caption saying the surrogate was fit and scored on the same items — here every one of the 30 fidelity cells is in-sample, and the Pareto figure then places an in-sample curve beside two out-of-sample baselines whose fitting sets differ, so the comparison is between reconstruction and generalisation rather than between methods.** This reads like a technicality and is not one: AUC 0.98 on the items you fitted a linear discriminant to is close to arithmetic, and the number that would actually license "the surrogate explains the model" is the same AUC on held-out instances. The rule is one clause in the caption we refuse to omit — *fitted on X, scored on Y, and whether they intersect* — plus the discipline of never drawing an in-sample curve and an out-of-sample curve on one axis without marking which is which. Under our setting this bears directly on any calibration-by-agreement study: if we fit a read-out to reproduce a model's behaviour and then report agreement on those same probes, we have measured our own optimiser, not the model. Coreference `arxiv-2611.17856` (an explanation scored against the evidence that produced it) and `arxiv-2611.10503` (a scope claim enforced by the objective rather than measured).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 324): **Pooling a nuisance estimate across groups is a bias-variance trade whose break-even point is a condition number, and this paper shows both sides of it with numbers: pooling scatter across 53 email labels buys +0.180 AUC where per-label covariances are rank-deficient (184,000× worse conditioned, ~64 positives per label in 1,001 dimensions), and costs 0.019 AUC on Genbase where the labels are near-orthogonal binary features that a shared covariance blurs.** Every estimate we borrow across strata to make it well-conditioned — a noise ceiling, a covariance for whitening directions, a shared decoder baseline, a normalisation constant — sits on exactly this trade, and the generalisable lesson is that the borrow is safe when the per-stratum estimate is underdetermined and unsafe when the strata differ in the *structure* the estimate is meant to capture. The operational form is cheap: report the condition number of both estimates per stratum group beside the downstream score, so a pooled estimate that silently degraded one group is visible as an anomaly in that group's condition number rather than as an unexplained dip in results. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20253` (a learned block the decoder never uses beside blocks that behave) and `arxiv-2611.20854` (a per-item difference the average erases).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 324): **Diffuse attribution is evidence about the model's reasons rather than about the explainer's quality, and the test that makes it a claim is cross-model: disagreement between classifiers' own internal attributions is low exactly where FLEX weights are concentrated (ρ = −0.568 on Enron, −0.545 on Genbase) while their *predictions* disagree on only 0.4–10.7% of instances — so a diffuse weight vector flags a decision reached by an arbitrary feature subset, not an unreliable explanation.** For us the mirror is direct: when two models, or two of our instruments, produce overlapping but non-identical direction sets for the same behaviour, the interior of that overlap is the content and the residual is the arbitrariness, and the honest report gives both. The construction worth copying is the concentration statistic as a *self-audit attached to the explanation* rather than a separate accuracy number — largest weight over mean weight costs one pass over the weights and can be printed in every read-out table. Its own limit is visible in the same table and must travel with it: with 6 to 32 labels per dataset, three of the five correlations are between −0.486 and −0.086 with p from 0.33 to 0.87, i.e. the sign is right and the evidence is not, and a claim of this shape needs the label count printed beside the coefficient. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing) and `arxiv-2611.20897` (a support set certified about the wrong object).

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 318 file-side / run 323): `arxiv-2611.21705` — Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models (Davide Liga — University of Luxembourg; Liuwen Yu — LIST; Matteo Magnini — University of Luxembourg; arXiv:2611.21705v1 [cs.CL], 2026-11-16, CC BY 4.0, pairs/ratings/code/dictionaries/results released). Full text via HTML (286K clean chars: §§1–9, references, Appendices A–J). **Substance:** a pre-registered design that makes "is this component moral?" falsifiable. 227 minimal pairs retained from 242 rated by five blind annotators (80 moral, 107 non-moral-standard, 40 descriptive; retention rule fixed before rating; α = 0.977 for which version is better), each shown in a cue frame, a no-cue frame and the bare original frame; fourteen models in base/IT pairs; ten located heads per model found by activation patching on 73 older moral pairs, then tested only on unseen pairs. Scored by share of each pair's total absolute head effect, pooled as a geometric mean of moral/normative ratios; controls are same-frame, and a mirror-image selection prices selection bias. Feature work on 14 TopK dictionaries (7 of the models) behind a capture gate; neuron lists selected and tested on disjoint halves; lens directions from category words only; ETHICS out-of-distribution; twins differing only in who bears the consequence. **Results:** pooled share ratio 1.00 [0.92, 1.07] with the cue and 0.90 [0.84, 0.96] without; per-model 0.83–1.22 / 0.70–1.08, none near 1.5; moral vs descriptive 1.19/1.09, normative vs descriptive 1.19/1.21, and the person/thing split accounts for all (no cue) or half (cue) of it; mean-ablation costs 23%/18% moral against 28%/21% normative, beating all 20 random sets in 10 of 14 models per frame, 37–39% on ETHICS against 1–3%; located features fire on descriptive pairs at 0.70–0.99 of their moral activation with the cue and at 1–33% without; every model names the annotators' standard 81–92% while its heads stay uniform; lens-direction removal costs 2–11% on moral pairs in 7 of 8 small models; one direction from normative pairs moves all three categories in all 14 models (40–240% of the gap), cosine 0.72–0.94 with the moral-pair direction; twins are judged more strongly for the moral member in 11 of 28 model×frame cells and less strongly in none.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 323): **Comparing raw intervention effects across two item families measures the families, not the units, and the numbers here are the cleanest case in the folder: 86–100% of heads in every base model have a larger raw effect on moral pairs, the raw test calls 47–100% of heads significantly different, and the ten "located" heads carry 1.3–2.1× share in 13 of 14 models once each item's effects are normalised to sum to one — so the offset is nearly universal and the discovery it produced survived only because the normalised statistic was checked separately.** Every component comparison we publish across conditions has this structure — a contrast set whose overall responses are larger, a per-unit effect that inherits the difference, and a ranking that then looks like specificity. The repair costs one division per item: express each item's effects as shares of that item's total, compare shares within and across items, and report the raw ratio beside the share ratio so the offset is visible rather than hidden. The companion detail is that the offset is *not* about the concept: a pilot with same-frame normative controls shows the raw ratio drop from 2.25 to 1.03 while the moral pairs are unchanged, which is the second use of the same number — it prices how much of a raw comparison was the item family. Coreference `arxiv-2611.17856` (a score certifying features against their own evidence) and `arxiv-2611.10503` (a scope claimed that the objective enforced).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 323): **A control set that differs from the treatment set in any dimension besides the one being tested counts that whole dimension as the effect, and this paper's own earlier controls were exactly that case: its original descriptive controls differed in the frame ("is typically" vs "is morally"), in the answer words (two bespoke lists per pair instead of one shared verdict vocabulary) and in the content (a thing rather than conduct), so the three-confounded comparison produced a raw ratio of 2.25 that a same-frame control erased.** The operational rule for us is to enumerate the dimensions along which the treatment and control items differ and to keep that list at exactly one — template, length, position of the edit, answer vocabulary, priming, token count — and where a confound cannot be removed, to say which cell of the result depends on it. The paper is unusually honest about the residue: "is morally" suits moral pairs better than "socially" suits etiquette pairs, "socially" sets etiquette pairs apart in 5 of 14 dictionaries, and a non-moral cue that fits a kind of norm does for that kind what the moral cue does for the moral pairs — which means part of every cue-dependent moral distinction may be cue fit rather than moral content, and no experiment in the paper separates the two. Coreference `arxiv-2611.06848` (a probe conditional on its extraction frame) and `arxiv-2611.20983` (a capability and a refusal separated so each is attributed).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 323): **Selecting units where one category puts its effect, then testing on fresh items of that category, produces an excess that survives the fresh-item test — so the mirror-image selection is not a refinement but the only thing that makes the excess interpretable: ten heads chosen on random halves of the moral pairs give a moral/normative ratio of 1.04 with the cue and 0.99 without, ten chosen on normative halves give 1.01 and 1.12, and only after that comparison does "no moral excess" become a result rather than a failure to find one.** This is the folder's selection-bias warning in its cheapest available form, and it inverts the usual direction of the worry: we normally ask whether a held-out test *confirms* a selected component, when the right question is what a selection run the other way round would produce on the same held-out items. The rule is two selections, two ratios, one sentence — and where the asymmetry is small enough to be noise the honest conclusion is that the selection procedure cannot distinguish the categories at all, which is exactly this paper's headline. The second half is the twin design, which does for items what the mirror selection does for units: hold scenario and edit fixed and change only who bears the consequence, so the component and the answer are compared on a contrast with one degree of freedom. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing) and `arxiv-2611.20854` (a per-item difference the average erases).

(1) **The factorisation is inside one model, not between two** — a per-dimension learnable gate, broadcast over tokens, splits the latent into a shared branch and per-model private branches, and two reconstruction terms (shared and total) make the branches compete so the private decoder cannot quietly take everything; that is a design we do not have and cannot get by post-hoc comparison. (2) **A cheap, checkable reuse test** — CLIP is unseen during training, only a single learnable linear adapter and a new private decoder are trained, convergence is 4–5 epochs, and the fidelity reached (total R² 0.72, shared 0.65) prices generalisation as how little may be retrained. (3) **The baseline mapping is honest** — because USAE/SPARC do not produce a shared atom, the paper maps their self-reconstruction onto GB-SAE's total and their pair-wise cross-reconstruction onto GB-SAE's shared-only, which makes the claim legible and narrow: total 0.60 is *not* better than USAE's 0.61, the shared-only 0.53/0.55 is what beats their 0.20/0.41. (4) **A private-branch qualitative read that has content** — ViT's private atoms read as class-discriminative textures and shape fragments, SigLIP's as language-tied prototypes, DINOv2's as geometry and layout, which is exactly the pattern each pretraining objective predicts. Its weakness is recorded in the entry rather than smoothed: sharedness is *entailed* by a Jaccard-alignment loss and only evidenced indirectly through retrieval, no independent per-model human read of a given shared atom is reported, the private branch contributes only 0.10–0.12 R² despite being argued as the residuals, the frozen random projector is never ablated, and the gate strength is named by the authors as having no principled selection rule.

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 317 file-side / run 321): `arxiv-2611.10503` — Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (Jinchi Zhu, Tie Luo — University of Kentucky; arXiv:2611.10503v1 [cs.LG, cs.AI, cs.CV], 2026-11-07, NeurIPS 2026, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence, ~19 MB source, code released). Full text via HTML (~80K clean chars: abstract, §§1–5, references, Appendices A–E). **Substance:** one sparse dictionary shared by several frozen vision backbones. Each backbone's final-layer features pass a frozen, orthogonally-initialised random linear projector into a common width (JL-preserving within-model geometry), then a *single* shared encoder with top-32 sparsification; a global learnable gate with one value per latent dimension (broadcast over tokens) softly splits dimensions into a shared branch and per-model private branches; one shared decoder reconstructs a common representation space and one private decoder per model reconstructs that model's private space; two reconstruction losses (shared and total) stop the private branch dominating, and a cross-model alignment loss pushes models to fire the same shared atoms — normalised shared activations, a continuous Jaccard over each model pair's supports, and a stop-gradient overlap weight on the magnitude difference across the overlap. AdamW, 30 epochs, batch 32, pre-computed features with three views per image, ~33 H200-hours for three backbones, three seeds for the reported averages. ImageNet-1K with ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2 (plus ViT/ConvNeXt/DINOv2 and all-four configurations at 10% of the data). **Results:** R² total mean 0.60 (ViT 0.56, SigLIP 0.58, DINOv2 0.65), shared-only 0.53 projected / 0.55 raw, private-only 0.10 / 0.12, private-on-residual 0.15 / 0.12; versus SAE 0.71 self (upper bound), USAE 0.61 self / 0.20 cross, SPARC 0.55 self / 0.41 cross; ConvNeXt configurations 0.63 total / 0.58 shared (three models) and 0.62 / 0.54 (four models, private up to 0.15 / 0.16); faithfulness with shared concepts close to total and above private and a random-orthogonal control, top-10 shared concepts reproducing the full dictionary's prediction in 62–88% and removing them in 26–48%; zero-shot shared-space cross-model retrieval beating all baselines by up to two orders of magnitude with private and projected features at the random lines; CLIP unseen, frozen encoder/gate/shared decoder plus one linear adapter and a CLIP private decoder converging in 4–5 epochs to total 0.72 / shared 0.65; linear probe on shared features 0.86 / 0.97 against 0.76 / 0.92 projected, 0.72 / 0.92 USAE, 0.78 / 0.93 SPARC; trained retrieval head instance R@1 0.99, category R@1 0.57, category R@5 0.81, mAP 0.48 against 0.96 / 0.48 / 0.75 / 0.39 projected; four-model zero-shot instance Recall@1/5/10/50 0.03/0.08/0.11/0.21 and category 0.06/0.13/0.17/0.29.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 321): **A concept claim carries a scope, and when the scope is enforced by the training objective it has to be measured separately or not claimed at all — here a cross-model alignment loss directly pushes different models' shared codes onto the same supports with the same magnitudes, and every piece of evidence that the resulting atoms are genuinely shared is indirect (reconstruction improved over pair-wise cross-reconstruction, hidden-model CLIP transfer, retrieval in the shared space); no experiment reads the same atom number in two models side by side and shows a human would give it the same meaning.** This is the folder's "a probe is a measurement, not the concept" lesson arriving on the dictionary side, and it applies to any claim we make that two of our instruments are measuring the same thing: a training signal that rewards agreement cannot also be the evidence of agreement. The habit to adopt is three-part reporting for a shared object — what the objective forced, what an independent measurement showed, and what the free (private) component absorbed — and the cheapest independent measurement available is the one this paper uses for generalisation rather than for sharing: hold the shared object fixed, adapt with as little as possible, and report what had to be retrained. Coreference `arxiv-2609.04344` (SharedSAE, a dictionary claimed across models) and `arxiv-2611.17856` (an explanation scored against the same evidence that produced it).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 321): **A factorisation's residual branch is argued rather than priced, and the numbers here show why that is dangerous: the private dictionaries are claimed to hold model-specific bias and are described per backbone with exactly the content each pretraining objective predicts (supervised textures, language-tied prototypes, geometric layout), yet they reconstruct only 0.10–0.12 R² while the shared branch takes 0.53–0.55 — so the qualitative story is rich where the quantitative share is small, and a reader has no way to tell "the private branch holds the bias" from "the private branch holds almost nothing, and the description is of the atoms that happened to survive sparse coding".** Every shared/private, invariant/variant or core/peripheral split we build has this structure, and the fix is one column: report what share of the total quantity the residual actually carries beside the qualitative account of what it contains, and report the same for an ablation that removes the residual entirely. The companion detail is that the private share *grows* with the ensemble (0.11/0.12 at three models, 0.15/0.16 at four) while the shared share shrinks (0.58 → 0.54) — a factorisation of this kind has a size-dependent boundary, so "these are the cross-model concepts" is a statement about a particular set of models rather than about the concept. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20253` (a learned block the decoder never uses beside blocks that behave) and `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 321): **A fixed random map between the model and the instrument is a design decision that needs its own ablation, and this paper's projector is doing load-bearing work that no experiment removes: every backbone's features pass through a frozen, orthogonally-initialised random projection into a common width, justified by Johnson–Lindenstrauss, chosen precisely so the alignment cannot be bought by a learned projection — but the paper never runs the same configuration with a learned projector, so the cost of the map (and how much of the reported fidelity is lost to it before the dictionary ever sees a feature) is unmeasured.** Two things travel with this for us. First, the geometric justification is real and worth copying: a random linear map preserves within-model pairwise distances, so a random projector is a legitimate way to put heterogeneous representations into one width — that is a reusable trick for any cross-model read-out of ours. Second, the control is cheap and its absence is the reason the paper's reconstruction ceiling cannot be interpreted: a learned-projector run would separate "the dictionary is limited" from "the projection is lossy". The companion detail is the honest baseline mapping the same paper does perform — mapping self-reconstruction onto total and cross-reconstruction onto shared-only — which is the right way to compare against methods that do not produce the same object, and its lesson is that a mapped comparison must be stated so the reader can see which column is meant to match which. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20854` (measurements written down before the experiment runs) and `arxiv-2611.20111` (a constraint whose applicability condition is a property of the input).

(1) **Explanation judged by forced choice under a similarity constraint, not by similarity** — two held-out images are required to be above the 99th percentile of random-pair dense similarity while being opposed in the feature's activation (low/high ratio below 0.15, high image above the 85th activation percentile), and a judge must name the one that will fire harder; that construction is what makes CLIP and IoU's flatness visible, and flat they are (0.204/0.202/0.202/0.202 and 0.240/0.234/0.248/0.232 across four evidence formats the behavioural test separates by up to eleven points). (2) **The edit is made attributable by construction** — the original patch token is kept and only the decoder-column difference `(γ−1)z_p,k·w_k` is added, so the 16,383 other dimensions' reconstruction error cannot enter the measurement, and the 80%-of-mass patch mask with a four-patch floor does the same in space; scale factors below zero then allow suppression past the original value rather than only switching off. (3) **A structured direction compared to a raw gradient under a matched budget** — the intervention magnitude is a fraction of the patch tensor's Frobenius norm precisely so that the dense baseline differs only in direction, and the round trip then shows dense steering's sign flipping at the larger strength (internal 342.5 → −18.5, final patch norm 16,024.6 against 1,448.0, MSE 5.5 × 10⁻² against 2.0 × 10⁻⁴). Its weakness is recorded in the entry rather than smoothed: agreement is 64.4% directional correctness on patch features (more than a third of interventions move the monitored feature the wrong way), the method needs a decoder trained on the representation, [CLS] evidence is one dataset and one encoder, the "reusable direction" claim rests on three illustrative images per feature, and there is no seed variance or significance test anywhere.

Frozen DINOv3-L/16 and SigLIP2-L/16 with BatchTopK SAEs — patch SAE on penultimate-layer tokens (1,024 → 16,384, k = 32, 100M / 25M token presentations), [CLS] SAE on the final block for DINOv3 only (1,024 → 4,096, k = 32, batch 512, 2M presentations, dead threshold 100,000); RAEv2 decoders. - Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 320): **An explanation score that measures similarity between a description and its own evidence is flat precisely where explanation quality changes, and the numbers here make the case unbeatable: CLIP sits at 0.204 / 0.202 / 0.202 / 0.202 and IoU at 0.240 / 0.234 / 0.248 / 0.232 across four evidence formats that a forced-choice behavioural test separates by up to eleven accuracy points.** This is the explanation-side twin of the folder's "a score can certify what a human refuses" line, and it applies to every explanation artefact we might report: a feature description, a circuit summary, a natural-language account of a probe. The metric is degenerate because it scores the description against the same activations that generated it, so any fluent description of the right region passes. The replacement costs one construction and no model training — two items that are near-identical in the model's ordinary representation but opposed in the quantity being explained, and a forced choice about which one the explanation predicts; the dense-similarity threshold (99th percentile of random pairs) is what stops the judge winning on coarse differences, and without it the benchmark measures category membership rather than explanation. Coreference `arxiv-2611.17856` (a faithfulness score certifying incoherent features) and `arxiv-2610.41661` (a perplexity check that cannot see the damage).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 320): **A direction derived from a gradient selects for local sensitivity rather than for presence, and the failure is arithmetic: at k = 128, 96.0% of the dimensions a sensitivity-only rule picks are inactive throughout the region they are applied to — so the intervention is spending its budget on components the current input does not use, which is why it looks fine at small strength and saturates almost immediately.** We do write probe-derived and gradient-derived directions of exactly this kind, and the diagnostic is one line: for the components an attribution ranks highest, report what fraction are actually active on the item, not merely influential in principle. The paper's fix is to rank by activation times sensitivity, and the reasoning generalises — sensitivity answers "would this matter if it were present", activation answers "is it present", and a steering direction or ablation set chosen on the first alone is a statement about the model rather than about the model on this input. The companion number is the top-attributed-versus-control separation that makes the ranking credible at all: 7.70 average target change for top-attributed dimensions, 0.23 for random active ones and 0.01 for bottom-attributed, at 1.94% / 0.20% / 0.02% per unit of intervention. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20253` (a learned block the decoder never uses beside blocks that behave) and `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 320): **A perturbation budget matched by norm and position separates "the direction is good" from "the direction is large", and this paper's clearest result only appears once that match is enforced: dense gradient steering and an attributed sparse direction receive the same injected patch change (140.8 at the small strength, 422.4 at the large one), after which the encoder amplifies the dense one roughly tenfold more (final patch norm 4,163.9 against 419.3, and 16,024.6 against 1,448.0), and the round trip then reverses its sign at the larger strength — internal 342.5 coming back as −18.5 — with image error over two orders of magnitude worse.** Every structured-versus-baseline comparison we publish has this trap, because the structured direction is usually a unit vector while the baseline is a raw gradient whose magnitude nobody normalises, so the baseline wins on volume. The three-line protocol: state what the budget is a fraction of, apply both arms to the same positions, and report the post-hoc quantity (the round trip, the re-encoded measurement) beside the immediate one — because here the immediate internal response ranks the methods in the opposite order from the quantity that matters. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20786` (an ablation that moves the physical quantity while fidelity stays fixed) and `arxiv-2611.20854` (a dataset average that erases a per-item loss).

- **Selection: the folder's first entry whose read-out is a per-TOKEN causal monitor trained in a regime where labels exist and deployed where they do not — and the first to price a dictionary not by accuracy but by the size and inspectability of the classifier built on it.** `2611.12935` earns the slot on four things. (1) **The transfer premise is an identity, not a hope** — in a causal transformer the hidden state at a token is computed the same way whether it was read in prefill or generated in decode, so the paper's question is precisely whether a monitor trained only in the labelled regime survives the unlabelled one, and it tests that against teacher-written text as the reference line so a decode drop can be attributed to the monitor or to the response. (2) **A selection-rule ablation that flips a conclusion** — summation reaches 94.3–96.2 macro-F1 on the 1B and collapses to 87.4 on the 4B GRU, and switching only the rule to the F-statistic lifts it to 96.4, which is the cleanest demonstration in the folder that feature-choice is a stronger lever than architecture (ConvNeXt best in six of ten rows, GRU spanning 87.4–96.8). (3) **A necessity test in three currencies** — the SAE buys no accuracy (raw states best in two of six cells, within 0.3 in three more) but keeps the detector at 1.4–3.6M parameters independent of backbone width against 7.6–20.7M, and every column is a named feature; that is a claim narrower and more checkable than "SAE features are interpretable". (4) **A robustness battery with the right control and an honest leak** — at most 5 macro-F1 lost under insert/remove/reorder, ConvNeXt at most 1.1, same-topic substitution as a negative control, while removal still puts 1–4% of tokens (7–8% on enterprise documents) on the deleted topic. Its weakness is recorded in the entry rather than smoothed: one seed per configuration and no significance tests anywhere, no "none" class so off-topic asides can be flagged only by a confidence drop (dynamic ConvNeXt at AUROC 54/51 cannot), decode scoring tests which topics appear and not where the switch is placed, and one synthetic seven-topic taxonomy on two backbones of one family.

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 315 file-side / run 319): `arxiv-2611.12935` — Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring (Rishikesh Mallagundla, Pranav Patel — Mercity; arXiv:2611.12935v1 [cs.AI, cs.LG], 2026-11-06, CC BY 4.0, 22 pages, 678 KB source, code/dataset/checkpoints released). Full text via HTML (~59K clean chars: abstract, §§1–6, Appendices A–C, references). **Substance:** a per-token topic monitor for a generating LM. A teacher model writes 10,000 synthetic prompt–response pairs over seven business topics, with topic spans marked in both prompt and response before generation (2.65 topics per record on average; 40% explicit, 35% light and 25% unmarked pivots among multi-topic records, so boundaries cannot be found from surface words). Frozen Gemma 3 1B/4B and Gemma Scope 2 SAEs (16,384 features, JumpReLU, l0_small) at ten late layers; feature reduction to 150 per layer by summation, F-statistic or group-lasso probe, or per-token dynamic top-k, or no SAE at all; then a small causal detector (3-layer GRU, 6-block dilated ConvNeXt with 379-token context, 2-layer causal Transformer, all width 256, AdamW, 15 epochs, best validation macro-F1). **Results:** prefill macro-F1 94.3–96.2 (1B, all inputs) and 87.4–92.4 (4B, summation) rising to 95.0–97.1 with label-based selection and 97.3 dynamic ConvNeXt; decode purity 90–98 with dynamic or label-selected features at both sizes and all three detectors, 69.4–75.8 for summation on the 4B; full coverage 95–99 on teacher text against ~30 points lower on the backbone's own text, 34–62 on four-topic prompts; at most 5 macro-F1 lost under the four perturbations, ConvNeXt ≤ 1.1, substitution control null, insertion AUROC 80–91 for GRU and Transformer but 51–54 for dynamic ConvNeXt, removal leak 1–4% (7–8% enterprise documents); no-SAE accuracy parity with 7.6–20.7M parameters against 1.4–3.6M, static inference needing 1.73M/3.84M encoder rows against 378M/839M for the ten full SAEs; worst-layer knockout 32.5 overlap points for summation versus 1.2 under the F-statistic on the same detector, summed knockout 124.9 → 4.2, layer ranks taken from knockout because attribution share tracks activation size.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 319): **A monitor trained where labels exist and run where they do not is tested by printing the same metric on a reference text and on the model's own, and this paper's table is the template: the identical detectors reach 95–99 full coverage on teacher-written responses and 64–78 on Gemma's own, a ~30-point gap that would otherwise be attributed to the detector and is instead attributed mostly to the backbone answering fewer of the requested topics.** Every read-out we deploy is trained in some labelled regime and evaluated in another, and the comparison we usually report is a single number from the second regime. The fix is one extra column: score the instrument on a text you know satisfies the property (the teacher's, the held-out labelled set, the unperturbed original) beside the text you care about, on the same metric, and let the difference between the two columns carry the monitor-error claim. It pairs with the same-topic substitution control in the same battery — a negative control that isolates capacity from contamination — and the honest leak the paper still prints (removal leaves 1–4% of tokens, 7–8% on its hardest topic) shows that a passing control and a surviving error coexist without contradiction. Coreference `arxiv-2610.41661` (a perplexity check that cannot see the damage) and `arxiv-2611.17856` (a faithfulness score certifying incoherent features).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 319): **Feature selection is a stronger lever than architecture in this table, and the same detector spans 87.4 to 96.8 macro-F1 across inputs — the 4B GRU loses 9 points to an unsupervised summation rule and recovers them under an F-statistic, a one-pass deterministic rule with no hyperparameters, while the three architectures differ by at most a few points within any row.** The general habit for us: when a read-out underperforms, the first ablation to run is the choice of *which* components feed it, not which classifier reads them, and the cheapest rule worth trying is a between-class versus within-class statistic rather than a top-by-activation one — because top-by-activation is a choice about magnitude that has no reason to align with the label. The second half is fragility: selection also decides how concentrated a read-out's dependence is, and the same summed-activation rule that costs the most accuracy costs 32.5 overlap points when its single most important layer is zeroed, against 1.2 for the statistic-based rule, so accuracy and single-layer fragility move together and a layer-knockout profile belongs beside the score. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20253` (a metric adjudicating in advance which representation shape counts) and `arxiv-2611.20854` (a per-item difference hidden by an average).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 319): **Attribution share and causal importance disagree specifically where activation magnitude is large, so the instrument ranked lower wins: gradient-times-input sums absolute contributions and gives a big-activation layer a big share whether or not the detector depends on it, which is exactly the layer the summed-activation selection rule favours, and the paper resolves the disagreement by ranking layers with knockout and using attribution only inside a layer.** This is the folder's repeat of "a read-out that accumulates magnitude measures magnitude", and it has a direct operational form for our probes and circuits: report a causal measure (ablation, knockout, patching) as the ranking of components and an additive attribution only as a within-component diagnostic, and print the rank correlation between them as the diagnostic's validity check rather than as a second opinion. The companion number is the within-layer version, which is where attribution does work — zeroing the ten highest-attributed features costs 0.1–10.3 overlap points against at most 0.16 for the ten lowest in all eighteen configurations, while about half of each layer's feature budget contributes little under the sparsest rule. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20840` (a relevance metric maximised over its own tuning parameter) and `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing).

- **Selection: the standing paired reading of `2611.01378` (JSD steering) taken now, precisely because its sibling in the hold list makes the comparison legible.** `2611.01378` had been held for several runs against the information-theoretic pairing; it is taken here on four things. (1) **The unit is a distribution, not a direction** — a dataset becomes an H-dimensional firing-*rate* vector (continuous probabilities, not binary firing), so the objective is a divergence between states of the model's whole feature economy rather than a between-dataset difference score, which is a structurally different read-out from every contrastive-steering entry in the folder. (2) **The response is analytic and cheap** — a sigmoid surrogate for firing probability gives a closed second-order form whose linear and quadratic coefficients depend only on SAE weights and both datasets' empirical rates, so the design is a small quadratic programme solvable without running the model. (3) **The off-target control is a hard filter, not a penalty weight** — a second divergence against a generic-language distribution defines a budget that *knocks out* candidates, which bounds the deviation by construction instead of trading it against the objective. (4) **A locality measurement with a matched ladder**: the teacher-forced versus teacher-then-free comparison at the same position over the same samples differs only in whether the fed-back token is the prepared one, and it shows the next-step internal state barely moves. Its weakness is recorded in the entry rather than smoothed: the method *loses* to a one-line prompt instruction on the two modes it handles worst, loses to the contrastive baseline on scope/applicability, has no seed variance or significance tests, and its 6-of-10 context-management feature reading is presented by the author as illustrative rather than as a characterisation.

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 314 file-side / run 318): `arxiv-2611.01378` — Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering (Hirofumi Morise — Ricoh Co., Ltd.; arXiv:2611.01378v1 [cs.CL, cs.LG], 2026-11-01, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence, 439 KB source). Full text via HTML (~96K clean chars: abstract, §§1–9 including Limitations/Ethics/AI-usage, Appendices A–L, references). **Substance:** steering designed as divergence minimisation rather than feature ranking. A dataset is represented by per-feature Bernoulli firing probabilities; the information a feature's firing carries about which of two datasets an activation came from equals the JSD between the two Bernoullis, and the sum over features is the dataset-level objective. Smoothing firing with a sigmoid and expanding to second order in the steering coefficient gives the change in firing rates as a function of the SAE encoder applied to the vector, with diagonal weightings from the firing probabilities, so the objective becomes a quadratic form in the decoded feature coefficients with coefficients computable from SAE weights alone. Vector construction is greedy: solve on the current support, add the feature with the largest objective decrease (rejecting candidates whose one-dimensional second-order coefficient is non-positive, i.e. an unbounded subproblem), repeat to a budget, and knock out candidates whose implied divergence cost against a generic-language reference exceeds a budget. A first-order variant drops the quadratic term. **Results:** Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, top-k 256 SAE at block 16 (H = 65,536, 3.3 × 10⁴ alive), 200 held-out items judged by Qwen3.6-27B against a fluency ≥ 4.5 gate — congruence 0.995 implementation, 0.970 consequences, 0.895 alternatives, 0.850 evidence, 0.700 criteria, 0.495 scope/applicability, 0.440 causes/background; the contrastive baseline beats it on scope/applicability (0.725) and prompt instruction beats it on criteria (0.895 vs 0.700) and causes (0.855 vs 0.440). Gemma-2-9B-IT with Gemma-Scope at layers 20 and 31 (format ≥ 4.9): 1.000 on causes and implementation at layer 31, 0.995 evidence, 0.965 alternatives, 0.960 consequences, 0.800 criteria; baseline's worst 0.595 and prompt's worst 0.255 on scope/applicability. Safety task on 100 jailbreak prompts with eleven 0–5 judge metrics: the first-order variant best on nine of eleven and ties on privacy, fluency 4.99 vs 4.76 unsteered, sensitive disclosure the flat cell (4.11 vs 4.07). Pulse experiment (SAEs at layers 16, 20, 24, 28, 31, 200 samples, four positions, teacher-forced vs teacher-then-free): parabolic divergence response at the injection layer persisting downstream with a stable minimising α, and a next-step response almost identical between the two conditions — so a single-token edit does not carry over and steering must be reapplied. Feature reading: 4 of the top-10 safety-task features fire on safety content or compliance stance, 6 on scope-control/interpersonal phrases; selected features spread through the interior of the (p_A, p_B) plane rather than off the diagonal. **Limits the paper states:** two models, one intervention layer each (two for Gemma), no sweep over extraction points, dictionary widths, sparsity or feature counts, entirely LLM-judge evaluation with custom rubrics, reference datasets model-generated and auto-filtered, non-monotonic budget behaviour explained rather than fixed, dual-use acknowledged.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 318): **A divergence between firing-rate *distributions* is a usable distance between interventions, and its two costs are the same two that make it useful: it is layer-relative (each layer has its own SAE, so absolute values cannot be compared across depth, only the shape of the α-response within a layer) and it is a proxy that can be optimised while the scored behaviour goes the other way.** The paper optimises firing-distribution distance toward a target dataset and then, on two of the seven modes, does worse than a sentence of prompt instruction — criteria 0.700 against 0.895 and causes/background 0.440 against 0.855 — which is the folder's standing warning in arithmetic form: the quantity in the objective is not the quantity in the table. For us the instrument is still worth keeping, precisely because it is distributional: our read-outs are almost all per-item or per-direction, and a dataset-level vector of firing rates gives one scalar for "how far did this intervention move the model's feature economy", computed without any generation. The rule to carry is to report the divergence *shape* (its minimum, its curvature, its curvature's sign) rather than a cross-layer number, and to print the behaviour metric beside it so the proxy cannot stand alone. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20840` (a relevance metric maximised over its own tuning parameter) and `arxiv-2610.41661` (a perplexity check that cannot see the damage).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 318): **An off-target control that removes candidates rather than penalising them is a stronger form of the same guarantee, and this is the cheapest instance in the folder: a second divergence against a generic-language distribution is turned into a budget, and any candidate feature whose implied deviation exceeds it is dropped from the pool before the vector is built — so the deviation is bounded by construction instead of traded against the objective by a weight nobody reports.** Every penalty-term design (KL weight, sparsity weight, fluency bonus) hides its trade-off inside a hyperparameter that is chosen after seeing both numbers; a hard budget cannot be traded away and makes the report's claim explicit ("no accepted feature costs more than this much deviation from general text"). The companion detail is the author's own honest statement that the budget does not behave monotonically — it filters one candidate at a time and is not a global constraint on the final vector — which is exactly the kind of caveat that separates a design rule from a guarantee. Coreference `arxiv-2610.41661` (a correction vector deliberately projected out of the behaviour direction before addition) and `arxiv-2611.00602` (a depth limit measured rather than assumed).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 318): **A single-token intervention does not accumulate, and the matched ladder that shows it is two lines of setup: run the model token by token on prepared text, inject at one position, then compare the next step when the prepared token is fed back against the next step when the actually generated token is — same samples, same position, only the fed-back token differing — and the two divergence curves come out nearly identical, so the changed token carried almost none of the shift forward.** For us this bounds any story in which an edit at one layer persists through generation; the correct statement is that the perturbation is local in the step, and steering (or patching) that is meant to hold must be re-applied at each step, which is what this paper does operationally. The second half is the width warning: the divergence read-out is itself computed over a four-token window, and the paper attributes the residual similarity in the teacher-forced condition to that window still containing the modified activation — a reminder that a read-out with a smoothing window will report persistence that is partly its own window. Coreference `arxiv-2610.41661` (a vector extracted from a shifted distribution carrying the shift) and `arxiv-2611.19972` (a state that is favourable in theory and rarely reached by training).

- **Selection: the standing carry that ran 3xx flagged as "the strongest off-target-slots candidate, to be taken later" — taken now, at full length.** `2610.41661` earns the slot on four things. (1) **The off-target effect is a fifteen-property profile, not a scalar, and the scalar is quantitatively exonerated**: 424 of 495 (model, dataset, dimension) tests are significant while the highest perplexity-versus-dimension correlation is 0.38, so the metric the field uses as its side-effect check provably cannot see the damage. (2) **A paired before/after rubric with a sign-agreement screen** — the judge is validated against a human only on the *direction* of the shift, screened at weighted κ 0.41, with PABAK substituted on the three dimensions too sparse for κ, which is the right agreement question when the claim is "this property moved in this direction". (3) **The retention test is a sign test on the intended decision, not a ratio** — behaviour is "retained" only if the logit difference keeps its sign, which is what exposes Qwen's formality addition (61.0%) that a 0.86–0.89 steerability ratio would have flattered. (4) **A contamination result the authors did not have to publish**: the repetition dimension had to be extracted from steered rather than unsteered generations and is the worst correction at 48% against 78% overall, attributed to entanglement with the behaviour direction where the behaviour and discourse vectors converge in later layers. Its weakness is recorded in the entry: one steering method (contrastive addition only), intervention only on samples that flipped between extremes (not identifiable in advance), one dimension at a time, moderate judge agreement (mean κ 0.48), and Gemma's add direction (62%) as the clear low cell.

- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 317): **A side-effect check built on quality is blind to the side effect's structure, and the numbers here are the cleanest separation in the folder: 424 of 495 (model, dataset, dimension) tests show steering moved a text property, while the correlation between perplexity and any of the fifteen properties tops out at 0.38 — so the field's standard "coherence did not collapse" check passes on runs that made the model less formal, less evidence-backed, more ambiguous and more contradictory.** This is the off-target twin of the folder's "a score can certify what a human refuses" pattern, and it applies verbatim to our own interventions: a probe-written edit validated by "the target logit moved and KL stayed small" has been checked with a scalar that cannot distinguish the intended change from fifteen unintended ones. The copyable instrument is a fixed rubric of output properties scored on paired before/after generations with the fraction of significant tests reported per property, and its cost is a judge pass and a one-time human sign-agreement screen — cheap relative to the intervention it is auditing. Coreference `arxiv-2611.17856` (a faithfulness score certifying incoherent features) and `arxiv-2611.20854` (a per-instance difference that the dataset average erases).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 317): **Retention of the intended behaviour is a question about the decision, not about the magnitude, and the sign test catches what the ratio hides: after correcting the discourse damage, per-sample steerability sits at a respectable 0.86–0.89 of plain steering, yet Qwen's formality correction keeps the steering's preferred option in only 61.0% of samples — the intervention did not weaken the push, it reversed it in two samples of five.** Every read-out we report after an intervention is magnitude-shaped (Δscore, fidelity, KL, recovered variance), and a magnitude metric pooled over samples treats a sign flip in 39% of them as a moderate average rather than as a failure. The two-line fix is to define retention on the per-item decision — did the item still come out on the side the intervention intended — report it as a fraction with the failure cell named, and never let a ratio stand alone as evidence the behaviour survived. The second half of the pattern is the direction asymmetry the same table exposes: correcting a property steering *removed* works 83% of the time, correcting one steering *introduced* works 74%, and for reasoning depth the split is 96% versus 63%, so an intervention's success rate is a function of which way the damage went and must be reported per direction. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20111` (strata that move +5.00 and −8.93 under a null average) and `arxiv-2611.20364` (a tie set that decimals conceal).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 317): **A direction extracted from the displaced distribution carries the displacement, and the paper's own worst result is the proof: the repetition correction had to be built from steered rather than unsteered generations, succeeds only 48% of the time against 78% overall, and the authors attribute it to entanglement with the behaviour direction — visible as behaviour and discourse vectors ceasing to be near-orthogonal in the later layers where mid-layer similarity is close to zero.** The general rule for our dictionary and probe work is to record the condition the contrastive set was drawn from as part of the instrument, because a vector built inside a steered, prompted or otherwise shifted activation distribution is partly a vector for the shift. The mechanistic detail worth keeping is that orthogonality is layer-local: two directions can be near-orthogonal where the intervention happens and converge downstream, so a one-layer orthogonality or projection test does not license the claim that the two effects are separable, and the projection variant in this paper (removing the behaviour component before adding the correction) is the right default rather than a refinement. Coreference `arxiv-2611.06848` (a measurement conditional on its extraction frame) and `arxiv-2611.20983` (a selector's capability and its refusal separated, so what was trained and what was not is stated).

Full text via HTML (~88K cleaned chars: abstract, §§1–5, references). **Substance:** a visual-analytics design study for auditing the *automated interpretation process* on SAEs — an LLM writes each feature's explanation and an LLM scores it, and the authors put a human at the diagnostic step with the workflow split into three single-question stages (structural soundness over decoder-similar feature pairs; explanation adequacy per feature; failure attribution into noisy activation / missed syntax / missed context), each stage a human-labelled seed set propagated by an SVM with prototype-first (TypiClust, 20 seeds), uncertainty-first and committee-disagreement-first seeding. One configuration throughout: Gemma-2-9b residual stream layer 31, 3,584 dimensions, 16,384 features, Neuronpedia evidence, 20 activating examples per feature over four activation-strength quantiles, three explainers (Llama 3.1 70B local, GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) and three metrics (fuzz, detection, embedding) with Llama as scorer, 0.5 as random baseline. **Results:** three experts completed the full pipeline in 127/112/132 minutes over 138/167/168 labels; end-to-end macro-F1 against a 233-feature adjudicated reference set was 0.36 for the score-only baseline, 0.40/0.37/0.41 for individual experts, 0.53/0.54/0.50 for expert pairs and **0.62 for the group of three**; the baseline reached 77% and 84% recall on the first two categories but only **10% on noisy activation** (58% of those features filed as well-explained), the experts 23–44%/55–75% and 67–87%; manual labels alone scored 0.60/0.65/0.63 while propagated labels scored 0.29/0.23/0.25; noisy activation was the dominant failure mode for all three experts, well-explained 45–51% of features, incoherent splitting rare (57/18/42 after propagation); inter-expert Cohen's κ .481–.663 with disagreement concentrated on Well-Explained vs Noisy Activation strictness; the expert who consulted explainer consensus clusters before the activating examples overrode three labels (anchoring), the two who induced the pattern first did not. **Limits the paper states:** adjudicated reference rather than ground truth, one SAE configuration, fixed explainers/metrics/thresholds/classifier, cold start and class imbalance, taxonomy not exhaustive (hedging, polysemanticity, readability outside it), less experienced users untested, no corrective loop implemented.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 316): **A faithfulness score can certify a feature whose activations are incoherent, because the explanation and its grade share the same evidence — the score-only baseline here terminates 58% of noisy-activation features as well-explained (10% recall on that category) while reaching 0.36 macro-F1, and the whole of the human's advantage sits in the category automation cannot see.** This is the sharpest instance in the folder of a metric agreeing with itself: the scorer is handed the same activating examples the explainer was, so a fluent explanation of a heterogeneous feature passes. Every read-out we build has the twin of this hole — a probe validated on the data its features were selected from, a circuit scored by the ablation that defined it — and the structural fix is the paper's: put the failure-source question in front of the number, so a feature must first pass "do these activations hang together" before its explanation is graded, and print the category distribution beside the score. The diagnostic question is one line: for the items our instrument marks confidently, what fraction were produced by a decomposition step nobody checked? Coreference `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing) and `arxiv-2611.20897` (a support set certified about the wrong object).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 316): **A failure can live in the relation between two components and be invisible in either alone, and this paper names the phenomenon and the detector: incoherent splitting is a boundary between two split features that falls on an arbitrary line rather than a conceptual one — one feature holding every "sta"-prefixed word except "state" — with each feature's own explanation faithful, so per-feature evaluation cannot find it and only side-by-side comparison of decoder-space neighbours can.** Our dictionary work assumes the opposite: that a feature's meaning is a property of the feature. The mechanical test costs one pass — take each entry's nearest neighbours in decoder space and ask whether the semantic boundary between them is one a human would draw — and where it fails, any downstream claim that reads the feature as a single concept (a probe on it, a steering vector along it, a downstream task using it) inherits the arbitrary split as noise. The companion point is that the paper's own screening threshold (0.40 cosine) is explicitly tuned for recall over precision, because the cost of missing a split is a whole feature set built on a broken unit while the cost of a false alarm is one inspection. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20253` (a learned block that the decoder never uses beside blocks that behave) and `arxiv-2611.20111` (a constraint whose applicability condition is a property of the input).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 316): **Evidence order is part of the instrument: the expert who read the model's consensus summary before the raw activations overrode three of their own labels, while the two who induced the pattern from activations first did not — same tool, same categories, different answer — and the authors' own repair is structural (force an evidence-first workflow) rather than a warning to reviewers.** For us the consequence is that a human evaluation pass that sees the model's explanation, its score, or its top-activating summary before labelling is a different instrument from one that does not, and the two must not be pooled; the same applies to our own QA, where reading a summary of a result before checking it re-anchors what counts as a discrepancy. The second half of the pattern is the propagation price printed honestly: manual labels 0.60–0.65, propagated labels 0.23–0.29, group 0.62 — so active-learning-style scaling is affordable for the coarse question (which module fails most, on which all three experts agreed) and not for the fine one (syntax versus context, resting on as few as two labels), which is the general shape of every selected-then-propagated set we report: it keeps its size and loses its content exactly at the finest boundary. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20445` (stable and uninformative) and `arxiv-2611.20678` (a learned last stage buying 0.09 of a 0.91 margin).

- **Selection: the strongest *held* item in the folder's own queue, taken at full length after nine consecutive declines — and the reason to take it now is that the batch commit falls due this run, so the entry that gets committed should be the one with the largest methodological payload.** `2611.06848` (Persona Perspectives) had been declined nine times as "readout-validity slot already filled", but its actual claim is narrower and more useful than that slot: it does not say probes are unreliable, it says a probe is a measurement *conditional on the frame it was extracted in*, and it prices that conditioning with a frozen-probe test that ordinary-item accuracy cannot see. Four things earned the slot. (1) **Re-extraction inside every condition** — word vectors and axes both rebuilt per persona, so the liberal-minus-conservative difference matrix is not contaminated by one condition's vocabulary. (2) **A three-rung predictor ladder with the ordering predicted in advance** — spillovers predicted by the persona's own geometry r = .59/.74, the assistant's .54/.64, the opposite persona's .44/.57, and the difference in geometry predicts the difference in spillover at r = .69 across 1,056 directed axis pairs. - Done 2026-11-17 (entry 313 file-side / run 315): `arxiv-2611.06848` — Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs (Austin C. Kozlowski — Knowledge Lab; Avital Mintz, Madison Lee — University of Chicago; arXiv:2611.06848v1 [cs.CL], 2026-11-04, CC BY 4.0). Full text via HTML (~61K clean chars: §§1–5, references, Appendices A–E). **Substance:** a geometric study of what a persona prompt does to a model's latent space. Word bank of 9,493 common words from 10,000 candidates × 33 contrastive semantic axes (ten anchor pairs each), both **re-extracted inside each of four system-prompt conditions**; all 528 axis cosine similarities collected per condition and the liberal-minus-conservative **difference** matrix correlated across 28 model pairs and against word2vec models trained from scratch on matched 69,087,676-token partisan corpora. **Results:** with no prompt the liberal–conservative and good–bad projections are unrelated (r = .02), .21 under the assistant prompt, .75 under the liberal persona and −.79 under the conservative one; the liberal–conservative axis re-angles most (liberal aligned with us .52, good .39, successful .40, strong .37, wise .39 under one persona and −.48, −.47, −.45, −.46, −.37 under the other, near zero unprompted), then collective–individual, soft–hard and feminine–masculine; reorganisation is absent early and appears by ~50% depth; difference matrices agree at mean r = .84 across the eight models and r = .64 (.67 for Llama 3.1 8B) with the partisan word2vec difference. Behaviour tracks geometry: off-target spillovers from steering ±0.33 residual norms along one axis while rating on another are predicted at r = .59 (liberal) / .74 (conservative) from the persona's own alignments, .54/.64 from the assistant's, .44/.57 from the opposite persona's, and the difference in alignments predicts the difference in spillovers at r = .69 over 1,056 directed pairs and 1,000 words. Monitors: three probe types (full-residual linear, eight SAE features at layer 19, hand-chosen anchor-word vectors) trained with no prompt on deliberately noncontroversial data hold 94–99% (truth) and ~99% (morality) on held-out ordinary statements under both personas — except the SAE truth probe, 97% → 88% under the conservative persona — while on 360 controversial truth claims and 300 controversial actions the same frozen directions read liberal-endorsed claims at 98% median "true" under the liberal persona and under 50% under the conservative one, and conservative-endorsed moral actions at 3–21% "acceptable" under the liberal persona against 67–97% under the conservative one. Statistics: topic-level sign-flip permutation (exhaustive 2^12 for truth, 99,999 draws for morality), Holm-corrected over 140 comparisons, article- and pair-bootstrap intervals, model behaviour cross-collected in open (rated by another model) and constrained formats. **Honest limits:** endorsement labels are model-generated hypotheses; word2vec ideology labels are outlet-level proxies and its hyperparameters were not preregistered; eight-model probe layers were selected on the ordinary test set that is then reported; SAE probes exist only for Llama 3.1 8B; the helpful assistant is the only non-political control condition; no mechanism for how a prompt re-angles the space.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 315): **A frozen probe is a measurement conditional on the frame it was extracted in, and the conditioning is invisible exactly where we usually test it: here three probe types hold 94–99% on ordinary true/false statements and ~99% on ordinary moral ones under both political personas, while the same frozen directions — pointing the same way in latent space in all three conditions — put liberal-endorsed truth claims at a 98% median under the liberal persona and below 50% under the conservative one, and conservative-endorsed moral actions at 3–21% acceptable under the liberal persona against 67–97% under the conservative one.** This is the sharpest form of the folder's recurring "a read-out is a measurement, not the concept" lesson, because the two halves of the evidence sit in one figure: ordinary accuracy, the number our probe tables always report, is completely insensitive to the effect, and only items whose expected label *moves with the frame* reveal it. The diagnostic to add to our battery costs one dataset — a set of items whose correct reading should change when the context changes (a negation, a role assignment, a stated premise, a system prompt), scored for movement — and the reporting rule is to print frozen-probe accuracy on ordinary items beside its reading on frame-sensitive items, never the first alone. Two companion habits travel with it: state the extraction context as part of the instrument (this paper re-extracts words *and* axes inside each condition, so its difference matrix is not contaminated by one condition's vocabulary), and where a probe's reading is shown, show the model's own behaviour on the same items beside it. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20983` (a selector's refusal half published) and `arxiv-2611.11398` (a control that decided which scores were artefacts).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 315): **A correlation between a geometry and a behaviour becomes a claim about the geometry only when the rival predictors are graded in advance, and the ordering here is the whole result: steering spillovers are predicted at r = .59/.74 by the persona's own axis alignments, .54/.64 by a neutral persona's, .44/.57 by the opposite persona's, and the *difference* between two personas' geometries predicts the difference in their spillovers at r = .69 across 1,056 directed pairs.** A single r against a single baseline cannot distinguish "the geometry explains the spillovers" from "any context-sensitive map correlates with any other" — the three-rung ladder can, because the middle rung is the same procedure under a neutral frame and the bottom rung is a frame that predicts the opposite ordering. This is the control structure our own read-out claims need whenever the explanation is a structure rather than a component: the mechanism's own geometry should beat a neutral frame and beat an opposing frame, and a flat ladder is evidence the claim is about the frame. The second half of the pattern is what makes the ladder worth running — the paper tests *differences* of differences, so shared variance between any two contexts cancels, and what survives is exactly the part the perspective changed. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20364` (nine of fourteen classifiers inside 0.12 points) and `arxiv-2611.21539` (the ladder from behaviour to probe to intervention).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 315): **One sentence of system prompt re-organises hundreds of pairwise relations at once and the re-organisation is shared across eight models from four families, which makes context a first-class variable in any claim we make about representation geometry rather than a nuisance to be averaged out: the liberal-minus-conservative differences in 528 axis alignments correlate at mean r = .84 across the 28 model pairs and r = .64 against word2vec trained on partisan text, the same axes that social science predicts should differ come out first (partisan affect, then egalitarianism-versus-individualism, then gender and soft–hard), and the effect is absent in early layers and emerges by roughly half depth.** For us the consequence is concrete and cheap. Every geometric statement our folder contains — "these two directions are related", "this feature's geometry mirrors that one", "the axis ordering is stable" — was measured under whatever prompt the evaluation happened to use, and this paper shows that a benign instruction moves those orderings in a structured direction. The habits to adopt are to report the extraction prompt as part of every geometric result, to probe at more than one depth because the effect has an onset, and to treat cross-model agreement of *differences* (not of raw geometry) as the evidence that a structure is real, which is what the r = .84 row licenses and what the paper is careful to say it licenses. Coreference `arxiv-2611.13548` (a denominator deciding what a number means) and `arxiv-2611.20786` (an ablation that moves the physical quantity while fidelity stays fixed).

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 312 file-side / run 314): `arxiv-2611.20854` — When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing (Taranum Wasu, Harsh Kashyap — Thapar University; HS Pannu — Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology, Patiala; arXiv:2611.20854v1 [cs.CV], 2026-11-16, 14 pages, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence). Full text via HTML (~23K clean chars: abstract, §§1–6, references). **Substance:** no learning anywhere. Six hand-written classical demosaicers over a Bayer RGGB mosaic (nearest, bilinear, colour-difference, Malvar–He–Cutler, Alleysson frequency-domain, Menon edge-aware as the expensive arm) on 80 benchmark images from Kodak (24), McMaster (18), BSD100 (20) and Urban100 (18), each placed in one of five visual content categories. A simulate–reconstruct loop (linear-light Bayer sampling → reconstruction → sRGB comparison, every preprocessing setting shared) measures PSNR, luminance SSIM, ΔE2000, edge preservation and an edge-localized artifact score; the per-image quantity of interest is the expensive method's PSNR minus the best fast-tier PSNR. Nine content descriptors were fixed on disk before the experiment matrix ran; correlations and a depth-2 decision tree were fitted afterwards, the tree under leave-one-image-out validation. **Results:** average ranking puts edge-aware first on every metric (PSNR 31.78 vs 30.40 Alleysson, artifact 10.48 vs 13.07) but the per-image gain spans −6.6 to +6.8 dB, mean +0.85 dB (t = 2.77, p = 0.007), and is ≤ 0 on 25/80 images (31%). Saturation predicts the gain at r = −0.86 (p < 10⁻⁶), colour variance r = −0.71, gradient std r = +0.36 (p = 0.001), saturation std r = −0.42. Category means: smooth +2.01, edge-heavy +1.89, repetitive/high-frequency +1.57, fine texture +1.32, high colour −1.56 dB (best-vs-worst t = 3.13, p = 0.004). Fast-tier win counts on PSNR: Malvar 35, Alleysson 30, bilinear 10, colour-difference 5; on edge preservation Malvar 61, colour-difference 18; on artifact score Malvar 50, Alleysson 26. Tree: 63.8% leave-one-out vs 43.8% always-pick-Malvar, +20.0 points. **Limits the paper states:** 80 images is modest, clean images only with PSNR primary, noisy capture untested, the recommender only chooses among cheap methods, a hand-tuned rule set was tried first and lost to the constant baseline, and errors cluster at the tree's own decision boundaries where the candidates are nearly tied.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 314): **A dataset-average ranking is a measurement of the average and nothing more, and the gap here is wide enough to matter: the same six methods that rank edge-aware first at 31.78 dB against 30.40 give a per-image gain ranging from −6.6 to +6.8 dB, with the ranking's winner a loss on 25 of 80 images — so the honest headline for a comparison is the distribution of the per-item difference and the share of items where it is zero or negative, not the mean and not the rank.** Every read-out table in our battery is built like the ranking this paper exists to replace: one number per instrument, an ordering, a winner. The three-line replacement is cheap — report the per-item difference against the *best rival* rather than against a fixed baseline (the paper's `gain` definition, which is what makes the negative tail visible), publish the fraction of items at or below zero beside the mean, and print the mean gain next to its spread so that "+0.85 dB" cannot be read without "−6.6 to +6.8". The sharpest single number is the third: on 31% of instances the expensive instrument buys nothing and costs an order of magnitude more compute, which is exactly the shape of a saturation claim for a probe that is slightly better on average and useless per-prompt. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20364` (nine of fourteen classifiers within 0.12 points — the same wide-tie distribution seen as a rank artifact) and `arxiv-2611.20111` (an aggregate that moves +0.07 points while its strata move +5.00 and −8.93).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 314): **Writing the candidate measurements down before the experiment is the cheapest substitute for a held-out explanation set, and this paper's credibility rests on exactly that: nine content descriptors with their definitions and thresholds saved to disk before the matrix was run, which converts a post-hoc correlation sweep into a pre-registered one and is why the r = −0.86 saturation line can be believed at n = 80.** Our selection step — which measurement gets to be the explanation — is run *after* the numbers exist, and the folder now has several entries whose lesson is that this ordering is the problem: a relevance metric maximised over its own tuning parameter, a support set that is stable and uninformative, an importance ranking read as causation. The copyable procedure costs one file: before the ablation battery runs, record the descriptors, the metric, the threshold and the split; then the report can say which of those were fixed and which were chosen after seeing data. The companion discipline is the paper's own disclosure that an earlier hand-tuned rule set lost to the constant baseline and was replaced by the data-derived tree — publishing the failed first rule is what stops a reader from assuming the tree was the first idea. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20840` (a relevance metric maximised over a tuning parameter with no held-out split) and `arxiv-2611.20445` (a support set that is real and explains nothing).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 314): **A correlate that comes with a mechanism story is still a correlate, and the mechanism here is stated rather than tested: saturation predicts the gain because the expensive method's advantage is interpolation along edges, so saturated low-structure images offer it nothing to exploit — but nothing in the design varies saturation with the content held fixed, so the category means (+2.01 smooth, −1.56 high colour) are consistent with that story and do not separate it from saturation simply co-occurring with the absence of edges.** This is the pattern the folder keeps meeting from the other side: a component located is not a component explained. For us the practical test is whether the correlate survives holding the competing factor fixed — if a probe's score tracks a surface property (prompt length, token rarity) and the story is "long prompts have more of the target behaviour", the experiment that earns the story is a matched set where length varies and behaviour does not, and its absence should be named in the entry rather than smoothed. The paper states its own limit plainly (findings suggestive, 80 images, clean only, mechanism inferred from assumptions), which is what makes the claim usable: the policy is offered as a selection heuristic, not as an account of the methods. Coreference `arxiv-2611.20441` (a component located is not a component explained) and `arxiv-2611.20786` (an ablation that moves the physical quantity while the image fidelity stays fixed — the opposite, and correct, way to earn a mechanism).
