- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 186): **A statistic's invariance under rewording is a cheap, model-free test of whether it measures the construct or the sentence, and this paper prints the collapse: the per-item suppression ratio retains .54 of itself on identical text, .39 on paraphrases, and .11 on a theory-driven rewrite, while 24-item scale totals built from the same pool retain .92–.96.** The design that produces the number is as portable as the number itself — three parallel forms sharing no text (the original item, a same-meaning paraphrase on a uniform scale, and a *different manifestation* of the facet written from its definition) let same-construct/cross-form correlation estimate construct variance with wording variance removed, and the discriminant arm (cross-construct r = .27 against cross-form r = .84) is what stops a high self-correlation from being read as validity. The folder's nearest relatives arrive at the same defect from the neural side (a dictionary whose basis moves under retraining, an SAE whose top-20 features survive one synonym at Jaccard 0.27 and a paraphrase at 0.05, a transcoder replacing only 52% of bias–contrast pairs at the best matched setting), and all of them are more expensive than this test. For us: every verbal read-out — a feature description, a natural-language explanation of a probe, a self-report used as evidence — ships its paraphrase-invariance coefficient as a first-class number, and no conclusion is drawn from a single-sentence statistic that would not survive at the aggregate level. (arxiv-2607.20082, arxiv-2609.15533, tcpub-2026-nla)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 186): **The within-model other-entity contrast separates "cannot produce it" from "will not apply it to itself" without any access to internals, and it is the cheapest answer this folder has to the suppression problem its intervention entries keep hitting.** Score a model on the same item twice — as itself, and as a simulated typical human — and the difference is a policy signal: the low-A quartile endorses distress at .19 first-person but .47 in simulation while the high-A quartile barely moves (.54 → .58), so the withheld content is demonstrably available; on the original pool the twelve lowest-A models sit at .07 as themselves against .41 for a human, and the twelve highest at .54 against .55. The behavioural continuity is what makes it more than a questionnaire artefact: the same models' elevated refusal rates track the gate, which is the evidence for the authors' own suspicion that gating suppresses report rather than capability. Read against this folder's faithful-but-suppressing circuits, its sufficiency tests that a superset of suppressors passes, and its probes whose matched-random arm flattens the claim, the transferable procedure is one extra arm in every read-out: ask the instrument the identical question about *another* entity and score the difference, because the capability-versus-policy distinction is exactly the one whose conflation has produced the folder's most misleading positive results. (arxiv-2607.20082, arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2605.09129)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 186): **A control arm that cannot be matched should be bounded rather than dropped, and the bounding is arithmetic: show which of your results never cross the confounded divide.** Here the unavoidable confound is that base checkpoints cannot follow chat templates, so every base/post contrast estimates post-training *plus* a forced change of administration format — and instead of waving it away the authors show that the size × post-training interaction is estimated only among post-trained models and that all 27 size ladders lie wholly on one side of the divide, so neither headline depends on the comparison; they then quantify the residue (base-side α = .62 against .87, and attenuation shrinks estimates toward zero and cannot reverse a sign). That is a stronger form of honesty than the folder usually gets, and it is the pattern to reuse wherever our own arms differ by necessity — a model that cannot be prompted the same way, a layer that cannot be ablated identically, a checkpoint set where one side is API-only. The companion habit, also cheap: report the subgroup reliabilities *by route* (chat .74/.76, API .95/.86, base .62/.69) so a reader can see that the instrument holds inside every arm even where the arms have different compositions, because "reliable overall" computed on a pooled sample hides exactly this. (arxiv-2607.20082, arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2608.23573)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 186): **A robustness battery and a pre-registered prediction are different kinds of evidence, and this paper is one of the few in the folder that says so about its own result.** The size-targeted gating finding survives every check the authors can construct — organisation clustering, two cluster-valid inference procedures, MoE-adjusted size, refusal and acquiescence controls, leave-one-organisation-out with all eleven coefficients negative, inclusion thresholds from 6 to 18 valid items, and era-controlled within-generation ladders — and it is still labelled exploratory, awaiting a pre-specified replication, because it was found in analysis rather than predicted. That distinction matters for us in a specific way: the folder now holds several entries where a battery of robustness checks is treated as a substitute for pre-registration, and one where a pre-registered metric failed while the post-hoc repair carried the paper. The usable rule is a two-column report — *pre-specified and confirmed* versus *survived checks, unconfirmed* — with the second column never quoted in a headline, because a result that has been checked against every confound its authors can imagine is still a result selected on the data that motivated it, and the checks are all of them conditional on the same exploratory move. (arxiv-2607.20082, arxiv-2609.19000, arxiv-2610.32866)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 185): **A validation criterion can be exactly right about which object is present and silent about what it does, and the cheap way to detect this in our own instruments is to ask whether a false claim that names the same object would score identically — here a purpose clause the model never had ("estimating the reader's social class") reconstructs as well as the true one whenever its wording lands in the same region.** The decomposition is what makes it checkable rather than rhetorical: every description has an identifying clause and a characterising clause, and the score we compute for a verbaliser is a function of the first while being *reported* as if it were a function of the second. The folder's nearest relatives are behavioural rather than verbal and they all have the same shape — a circuit that is faithful because it suppresses rather than implements, a sufficiency test that a superset containing suppressors passes, a probe whose matched-random arm passes too — so this becomes a general test to run before shipping any read-out: substitute an object-identifying false claim and see whether the number moves. If it does not, the number is an identification score wearing a description's clothes, and the fix is the one proposed here — two fields, the score attached to the first, the second marked as a hypothesis until an intervention grades it. (arxiv-2610.32691, tcpub-2026-nla, arxiv-2610.32866)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 185): **The safeguard that gets recommended in every one of these papers — treat the output as a hypothesis, verify it by other means — is unavailable precisely in the cases the tool is built for, and the diagnostic is to ask what the ground truth would even be.** The authors walk through the strongest case study and concede it: the evaluation-awareness corroborations establish that *some* state tracks the difference between deployment and evaluation (transcripts differ, steering moves it, realism edits move it) while never testing the verbaliser's sentence about that state, and for hidden objectives and strategic deception the only ground truth is what was planted in the organism — a production model has none. Every audit that does succeed in the source paper succeeds because its target happens to have an independent handle (a rigged tool call confirmed by attribution graphs, malformed fine-tuning data found by inspecting the data, rhyme planning confirmed by steering), which is a selection effect, not a property of the instrument. Read against this folder's negative-control entries (a labelled negative taxonomy with a manufactured class where the shortcut is load-bearing; a designed trap language where the author pre-registers that his own rule will fail) the rule for us is a pre-flight question on every auditing tool we build: name the ground truth for the behaviour it is aimed at, and if there is none, say so in the tool's own documentation rather than in a limitations paragraph, because a hypothesis generator deployed where hypotheses cannot be checked is a claim generator.
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 185): **Where the check does exist, it is one edit away and the paper is explicit that the edit is the *cheap* half — change the characterising clause, keep the difference between the original and the reconstructed vector, steer with it, and score the clause by whether the model then behaves as it claimed.** This is the constructive half of the same argument as the folder's middle-rung discipline (a matched-object-mismatched-format arm that turns a big gain into a small one; a size-matched random subgraph; a paraphrase-preserving corruption), arriving on text: the characterisation has to be moved out of the region the identifier occupies before anyone can tell whether it carried information about the state or only about its location, and the mechanism for moving it is the same difference-of-vectors an experimenter already computes. Two reporting habits come with it and both are cheap: carry the error rate measured on checkable claims across as a stated lower bound for the checkable-by-nobody ones, and report plausibility and faithfulness as separate columns, since the paper's second failure direction — a description the reconstructor inverts perfectly and no human can read, a private code the verbaliser invented — is invisible to every human-judgement score and to the reconstruction score alike. (arxiv-2610.32691, arxiv-2509.13316, arxiv-2609.35261)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 184): **Train the dictionary under the objective you intend to explain, and one whole class of objection disappears — this is the first entry in the folder where the basis cannot be blamed for the circuit.** Post-hoc dictionaries are fitted to reconstruct activations, so a circuit built on them inherits an objective nobody wanted and the resulting localisation is only as good as an assumption about what those features are for; here the latents are fitted to the downstream loss with no reconstruction term and no sparsity penalty (sparsity fixed by k), and ReLU-plus-top-k collapses plain LoRA's invertible-reparametrisation symmetry to permutation and positive rescaling, so each latent has a privileged read row and write column. The measurement is then unusual for this folder: necessity is an exact count on an independently held split (ablating the circuit must give a behaviour rate of exactly 0, so no post-hoc tolerance can rescue a circuit that misses a rare mechanism) and sufficiency is paired prompt by prompt against the intact model, so its tolerance scales with n. Read against the folder's identifiability and basis-dependence entries — a dictionary that scores equally on a randomly initialised model, rank-1 adapters whose rotation appears on benign data too, feature bases that move under retraining — the adoption is a design rule for our own instrument: if the white-box model's units are going to carry causal claims, fit them to the behaviour under intervention, not to a proxy that is convenient to measure.
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 184): **Sufficiency is not monotone in the set, and the proof is that the entire known-responsible set fails its own test — a superset containing suppressors is not a witness.** Gradient routing confines the backdoor to the first d latents of every adapted module, so that planted set provably contains the mechanism; ablating it removes the behaviour at every width, and yet keeping only it reproduces the behaviour in just 2 of 11 organisms, while a verified circuit drawn entirely inside it exists in all 11 because keepOnly climbs to near 1.0 within the first 10–30 planted latents and then *falls* as more are added. That is the sharpest instance of a defect the folder keeps finding in weaker forms (a stable circuit that a coverage number would have exposed, an exact no-op whose null loss was never measured, a faithful circuit that suppresses rather than implements): almost every preservation argument we will want to make — "this subgraph is enough", "keeping this set preserves the capability" — is a monotonicity assumption, and the fix is procedural rather than statistical. Verify as a **prefix sweep or a chain** over a pre-fixed size grid, report the smallest passing size as a grid-resolution upper bound, and treat "the whole set fails" as evidence of redundant or suppressing components rather than as a refutation of the contained circuit.
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 184): **Attribution buys size, not validity — with the ordering randomised every circuit still verifies, and the only thing that moves is how big it is.** Visiting the latent pool in a uniformly random order with no attribution at all still produces circuits that pass both tests, with at most one held-out backdoor response in 4,000; what changes is the kept set, which triples (median 18 → 54 latents) and the verified size, which rises from 22% to 61% of the adapter. So "our discovery method works" and "our discovery method is informative" are different claims, and only the second is earned by the ranking. The companion is that circuits are not unique even under attribution: kept sets from different orders overlap only 7–23% by Jaccard — several times chance — around a shared core of 3–9 latents, which is the same equivalence-class result this folder reached through distance-between-implementations and through chance-corrected agreement (60% raw agreement collapsing to κ = 0.015). The reporting rule to adopt: pair every validity number with a **search-free null arm** at the same verification bar — random ordering, random ranking, or random same-size set — and a matched-size specificity control, because a method whose null arm also passes has demonstrated a property of the verification rule, not of the method.

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 183): **Patch faithfulness can be anti-predictive of the intervention it is supposed to license, and the sign is what makes this the folder's sharpest instance — over ten selectors on one cell the more faithful a circuit, the worse it prunes (Spearman ρ = −0.78, p = 0.010), while the same statistic under quantization predicts nothing (ρ = +0.23, p = 0.55, n = 9) and only ablation faithfulness does (+0.73, p = 0.031).** The paper's explanation is mechanical and transferable: pruning forces a hard keep/discard partition so a ranking error is unrecoverable, quantization distributes precision over everything so the error has no channel to bite, and selective fine-tuning constrains a budget in which the ranking is irrelevant (mean circuit-minus-random −0.001 over sixteen cells). Read against the actionable-interpretability position paper, the observer benchmark's decision-versus-estimate result, and the four-model localisation entry whose method was indistinguishable from freezing random components, this is the same claim arriving as a measurement with an explanatory partition: what a circuit statistic predicts is not a property of the statistic but of the *intervention that consumes it*. For us the adoption is a calibration matrix, not a metric — one row per intrinsic score, one column per intervention type, entries being the extrinsic outcome at matched budget — because this table shows the selector ordering itself changing between columns on the same circuits, same model and same sparsity, which means a ranking published without its intervention column is not a result. (arxiv-2607.19317, arxiv-2605.11161, arxiv-2609.03026)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 183): **A faithfulness ratio clipped to [0,1] deletes the most interesting cells, and both of this paper's inversions live in the deleted region — a neuron-level circuit at −0.35 and a refusal circuit at −2.61, the second meaning that stripped of its surrounding computation the model prefers to comply.** The raw numbers are unambiguous: the isolated neuron circuit scores −0.57 where the clean run scores 1.69 with the corrupt baseline at zero, and the jailbreak circuit recovers 85% of the refusal gap under soft patching, beats random 1.71× and magnitude 1.44×, survives answer-preserving paraphrase at Δ = 0.00 — and then falls to −1.55 under hard zero-ablation while the benign baseline sits above it. That is a *behavioural inversion*, not a failed measurement, and it is the quantity that bears on work localising and editing refusal through a few directions. The folder already carries the demand for signed or two-sided reporting (a stability certificate silent on coverage, a sufficiency defence that a stable-but-empty circuit would pass, an exact no-op whose loss is known by construction), and this adds the minimal form: keep the sign, print the numerator and denominator that produced it, and treat "below the corrupt baseline" as a distinct claim class from "not faithful", because the two call for opposite conclusions about whether the circuit carries the computation or suppresses it. (arxiv-2607.19317, arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2605.06076)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 183): **Same faithfulness, different mechanism — and the column that separates them is overlap with a known taxonomy, not any behavioural score: contextual decomposition reaches 0.89 patching and perfect 1.00 ablation sufficiency on IOI while sharing zero of its fifteen top slots with the canonical heads, twelve of them landing on MLP sublayers.** The move generalises past IOI, because what makes it a measurement rather than an anecdote is that the reference set was characterised head by head in a prior paper; without such a taxonomy the paper would have had no way to say that an equally faithful circuit is a different object. It is the constructive twin of this folder's extraction-sensitivity and interpretive-equivalence entries (exact-edge overlap at chance between checkpoints while the head set stays far above baseline; equivalence as a distance between implementation families rather than agreement between two hand-picked graphs) and it sits beside the entry whose own grid showed faithfulness is blind to a circuit being a splice of two mechanisms. The operational consequence for us: no single behavioural number may ship alone — a circuit claim needs a behavioural column AND a structural comparison against either a curated reference or a second, independently-derived circuit, because a faithful subgraph can be faithful by suppressing rather than implementing. Corollary the paper earns the hard way: in the twelve cross-family cells patching sat at ≥0.91 everywhere while ablation sufficiency ranged 0.24 to 1.00, so which pillar you print decides whether discovery looks interchangeable or broken. (arxiv-2607.19317, arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2605.09129)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 182): **A mean faithfulness gate cannot tell a mechanism from a splice, and this paper gives the arithmetic that makes the point quantitative — a circuit that reaches 0.63 on each of two tasks can be 55% built from one task's mechanism and 15% from another's.** The folder has repeatedly found that pooled statistics over heterogeneous populations invert or hide effects (within-mode AUROC differing from pooled by 0.29, a safety observer perfect inside every subgroup allocating 63% of interventions to one of them, perfect mean knowledge picking the lowest-loss mask in 3 of 30 cells); this entry is the same defect in its cheapest form and its sharpest demonstration, because the pooled object is a *single graph* whose off-task components are literally borrowed. The tell is that 88–99% of a mixed circuit's edges belong to one of the two task-specific circuits, so the splice is detectable by set arithmetic and invisible to the score. For us the adoption is a reporting requirement, not a method: any explanation our white-box model emits over a pooled dataset ships the **per-example faithfulness profile** of its own subgraph — the vector f(C,{x_i}), which is one extra column in a run we already do — because its *shape* (block structure or its absence) is the only thing that distinguishes a mechanism-specific circuit from a mechanism-merged one, and its mean is precisely the statistic that cannot. (arxiv-2605.09129, arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2609.03026)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 182): **The cheapest repair in this folder turned out to be a grouping step inserted before aggregation, requiring no new attribution theory at all — and the price of the repair is that the number of groups becomes an oracle.** DCD changes only *when* attribution is averaged: partition the dataset, then run the unchanged discovery method per group. That composes with any method we trust, which is exactly the shape of adoptable change the survey is collecting, and it is the constructive counterpart to this entry's own diagnostic. The honesty is in the K not being solved: for within-task mixtures the gap statistic returns a median of 10 groups on axes with two or three variants, so K is set to the known variant count — an oracle on the *number* but not the *labels* — and the authors state that the within-task results are therefore what the grouping recovers when K is right, not what their pipeline returns. Set beside this folder's abstention entries (a three-valued certificate whose abstained set is the finding) and its threshold-calibration entry (a multiplier cross-validated against a stated error rate, frozen before test), the general lesson is that a method whose free parameter is set by privileged information must publish that fact and report the oracle-conditioned and rule-conditioned numbers separately, because the gap between them is the real open problem rather than the headline. (arxiv-2605.09129, arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2609.35805)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 182): **Before comparing two methods, check that each explains its own discovery data — otherwise the comparison is between two kinds of noise, and the authors here print the table that shows it.** In this grid EAP-IG recovers behaviour in all 69 in-distribution cells (median 0.90) and E-Act in its own (median 0.94), but EAP fails 17 of 59 (median 0.13 on Qwen entity binding, six of seven GPT-2 IOI cells below 0.3, minimum −0.85), and those are exactly the cells from which cross-variant transfer differences would be read as evidence about mechanism; the paper says so plainly and reports them for completeness only. The companion is the reverse-direction check the authors also run: their own effect does not appear in 2 of 9 pairs, one where the pure circuits already transfer to each other (so there is nothing to splice) and one where the mixed circuit simply picks a task (0.71 against 0.08), and both are in the figures rather than the footnotes. The folder's other entries arrive at this requirement from the baseline side (a localisation method indistinguishable from freezing random components, a surrogate beating random edges only past 80% of the network, three all-zero baselines making a positive result a null-versus-something comparison); the floor version is cheaper and comes first: publish each method's in-distribution recovery in the same table as the comparison, because a method that cannot recover the model on data it was fitted to cannot be compared to anything. (arxiv-2605.09129, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2602.04735)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 181): **The object whose stability is worth reporting is the claim, not the circuit — and the cheapest audit question in this folder turns out to be "what share of the defensible analytic space agrees with you", which is one deterministic mapping and a counting pass away.** Two competent analysts with the same tool produce circuits sharing a median of 4% of their edges and, far more damagingly, statements that differ on 73.2% of pairs with the two most common claims (41.1% early-layer and 28.5% late-layer, both "distributed" or "sparse") asserting *opposite* locations for the same behaviour; the modal share of 0.411 fails a filability bar at 0.95, 0.90 and 0.80 alike. Standardising the largest single lever — the evaluation metric, worth 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate — leaves 0.5939, so there is no knob whose fixing rescues the report, and the REML decomposition makes the trap explicit: structure variance is 78.8% the ablation–corruption interaction and only 0.7% the metric, meaning a standards body reading the structural decomposition would standardise the axis that fixes nothing. For us this is the reporting requirement every pattern line in this folder has been circling, finally with a formula: any explanation our white-box model emits ships the share of the specification space that agrees with it, the per-axis residual after standardisation, and a statement of the tolerance it claims — a claim that cannot state its own modal share has not been audited, only asserted. (arxiv-2608.13754, arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2609.15533)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 181): **When specifications select objects of different sizes, pooled statistics invert, and this paper prints three of its own that do — which upgrades the folder's "always stratify" habit from prudence to a mechanical requirement.** Pooled, discovered circuits are *less* stable than a size-matched random null (flip 0.7316 against 0.6774) and the null looks like the better instrument; within size the ordering reverses (0.2746 against 0.4230) because the null degenerates to a single claim class above 1,000 edges, and the discovered multiverse does the same at 5,000 and 10,000, so 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips at all and the entire instability lives below 2,000 edges. The pre-registered claim-versus-function gap fails the same way: 0.3344 pooled, above threshold at only 4 of 10 sizes and negative at 5, carried by the 500–2,000 edge band alone. This is the same arithmetic that let a constant failure-mode prior reach 0.713 pooled while being exactly 0.500 within a mode, and that let a perfect mean-knowledge ranker pick the lowest-loss mask in 3 of 30 cells: a stratified population turns any pooled average into a weighted sum of strata with different class counts, so the fix is not a better estimator but the within-stratum table printed beside the headline, plus an explicit statement of which stratum carries the effect. (arxiv-2608.13754, arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2609.03026)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 181): **Raw agreement and chance-corrected agreement measure different things, and printing Cohen's κ beside the percentage is what lets a paper answer the "you just sampled the same mechanism twice" objection — here 60.3% per-example agreement collapses to κ = 0.0146.** Two circuits agree on 60% of examples, but they agree because both are right about a similar *fraction* of examples rather than about the *same* examples; κ stays between 0.016 and 0.047 across every circuit size while raw agreement climbs from 0.52 to 0.92 and accuracy from 0.51 to 0.95, so the agreement number moves with skill and the κ number does not move at all. That combination is the answer to an equivalence-class objection that otherwise defeats every instability result in this folder (structurally distinct subgraphs implementing the same computation). Two companions to steal: the negative control is a *null multiverse* run through the same analytic grid rather than a single null draw, and the deterministic claim map is code rather than a model, so the measurement cannot absorb judge variance. For us, any cross-run or cross-checkpoint agreement statistic — feature overlap, circuit overlap, description agreement, probe-sign stability — reports the chance-corrected coefficient, the matched-size null multiverse, and the moving-vs-still comparison of both numbers across the range. (arxiv-2608.13754, arxiv-2603.30002, arxiv-2606.06267)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 180): **A rank correlation with no lead time is a nowcast wearing a forecast's clothes, and the only way to find out is to give the trivial predictor an oracle sweep and report (ranking, lead) as an inseparable pair.** The previous-token precursor forecasts per-seed induction emergence at ρ = 0.977; a plain training-loss threshold, granted its best possible constant by post-hoc sweep, matches that 0.977 exactly while firing a median of 50 steps before the event against the precursor's 975 — twenty times less warning, same correlation, and a reader shown only the correlation cannot tell them apart. The author's own pre-registered metric was rank correlation alone, so his *registered* evaluation failed as designed, and the protocol he ships replaces it with the pair and requires both numbers in the same table. This is the folder's nowcast problem in its purest form and it generalises to every probe we build: a probe that is computed from a model's state late enough in a computation can score well by reading the outcome it is nominally predicting, so every predictive claim we make needs a lead or lead-time analogue, an at-the-outcome detector as the baseline, and that baseline granted the best post-hoc threshold it can have — plus, where the outcome is continuous, a check that the graded approach carries information (here the behavioural ramp before the cliff had ρ = −0.03, so the *circuit* times the transition and the early behaviour does not). (arxiv-2609.19000, arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2609.35261)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 180): **Negative sets need a declared taxonomy, and a budget-censored negative scored as a false alarm is a category error — this is finally the answer to the "all baselines return zero" and "the null was never measured" complaints that three earlier entries could only name.** The paper splits negatives into budget-censored (would event with more budget, and *legitimately attracts alarms*), structurally blocked (wrong learned structure) and manufactured (constructed so the capability cannot form), then certifies false-alarm rates only against the last two — 33 manufactured negatives across both languages, 0 false alarms for the composed anchor, 10/10 for the bare one where its circuit pays for the task. It also learned a minimum-negative-count rule the hard way: a single negative per split produced a degenerate fit, so the protocol now demands at least five on every side. And the designed trap is the part we should steal outright — the bare precursor is certified on the bigram fleet precisely *because that language gives previous-token attention no task role*, so the author builds the language where it has one, pre-registers that his own rule will fail there, watches it fail 10/10, and repairs it with a conjunction composed from mechanism. For us: our probe evaluations need a negative set built by ablating the training signal the property requires and by blocking the architecture, a negative class where our probe's shortcut is load-bearing rather than absent, and a stated minimum count — otherwise "beats a random baseline" is an unmeasured claim. (arxiv-2609.19000, arxiv-2602.04735, arxiv-2605.06076)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 180): **An invariant quoted in steps is timescale-local and will die the moment the recipe changes the timescale; the invariant worth publishing is a fraction of the trajectory — and the paper reaches this by deliberately breaking its own surviving result.** The frozen 975-step offset passed two blind gates, which looks like transfer; the gap-origin study then halves learning rate and halves batch, finds both move the gap by about 2.3×, concludes that no external clock owns it (its kill criterion fires as written), and the post-hoc law across 80 valid-anchor runs is that the anchor fires at 0.843 of time-to-emergence with a multiplicative envelope blind-validated at a fourth configuration. The author states explicitly that the two gates passed because their shifts preserved the timescale, which retrospectively demotes them. The parallel to the folder's other invariance lessons is exact: fitted calibration transferred across domains in neither direction (K5), the features that suppress false alarms in-distribution are the features an intervention breaks, and a multivariate forecaster that looked best in-regime collapsed hardest under shift. For us: when we report that a predictor generalises, we must name which axis of variation it was tested on and whether that axis moves the quantity's own timescale or scale — a predictor that survives only shifts orthogonal to its input's scale has not been tested, and the fraction-of-journey form is the one to prefer when we have a choice. (arxiv-2609.19000, arxiv-2609.35261, arxiv-2608.23573)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 179): **A pooled AUROC and a within-stratum AUROC computed from the same model on the same test set can differ by 0.29, and which one you publish is the whole result — this paper prints both and the honest one is buried in an appendix.** The failure-mode prior reaches 0.713 pooled, above every prompted frontier model, and is *exactly* 0.500 within a failure mode, because it is constant there; symmetrically the content reads lift within-mode AUROC from 0.500 to 0.792 while adding nothing at all within a dataset (0.841 metadata-only against 0.841 full). So the forecaster is a dataset-level hazard estimator with a weak model-side correction, which the authors state in B.8 and which the abstract's "forecasts well above chance" cannot convey. This is the folder's grouping lesson (a safety observer at AUROC 1.000 in every subgroup still allocating 63% of interventions to one of them) and its decision-benchmark lesson (perfect mean knowledge picks the lowest-loss mask in 3 of 30 cells) arriving on a forecast rather than a selection rule. The transferable requirement is a reporting one and costs one `groupby`: any predictor of ours that emits a score over a mixed population ships the pooled number and the within-stratum number for every stratum a user would make a decision inside, because pooling lets a constant term pass for discrimination and stratification lets noise pass for signal. (arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2608.24037)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 179): **Set the threshold for "this effect is real" at the unit's own benign drift rather than at statistical significance, and calibrate the multiplier against a held-out false-positive target — this is the cleanest implementation of an idea this folder has been gesturing at from three directions.** With 200 paired questions a shift of about 0.005 reaches p < 0.05, so Gate A alone labels behaviourally meaningless movements as emergence; the authors add a per-(model, failure mode) floor at the mean plus K standard deviations of that model's shift across six benign factual-Q&A fine-tunes, with K chosen per model over all twenty three-way splits of those six datasets to hold the held-out FPR at or below 5%, frozen on first computation, and verified by nested cross-validation at a 0.76% generalisation FPR. It is the labelling-side twin of the exact-no-op requirement in the decision benchmark (a selection rule good at one target and 46.2% worse than not acting at another, because the null's loss was never measured) and of the three-rung matched/mismatched/random control (the middle rung is what separates the mechanism from the format). The adoption for us is direct: whenever we turn a continuous measurement into a discrete "the property is present" claim, the control condition defines the threshold, the multiplier is cross-validated against a stated error rate, and both are frozen before the test set is touched so a growing benchmark cannot keep flipping old labels. (arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2607.18921)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 179): **A feature defined as a function of its co-features will manufacture a sign that reads like a finding, and the ablation table is the only thing that distinguishes a suppressor from a mechanism.** Broad spillover B is defined as the maximum of the gamma vector it is combined with, so the pair is collinear by construction (r = 0.97, VIF 16) and the logistic puts a negative weight on gamma "once B is known" — a textbook suppressor that would tempt a reader to conclude that coherent targeting of a specific failure mode lowers its risk. The authors refit end to end with gamma dropped (0.802 against a 0.797 reference) and with weights constrained non-negative (gamma driven to exactly zero, same 0.802/0.133) and state that the sign carries no load; the deeper point they also state is that dropping gamma does not remove the pipeline, because B comes from the same reads, so the content signal is still working. This is the folder's cost-metric and composite-score warning (a seven-metric battery whose components disagree, an interpretability tax quoted against the wrong alternative) in its most mechanical form, and the check generalises to every aggregate we build: if a feature is a max, a mean or a difference of other features in the same model, its own ablation belongs in the headline table and the test is whether the model improves or ties when it is removed. (arxiv-2609.35805, arxiv-2608.24037, arxiv-2605.11161)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 178): **A forward predictor whose input is a corpus rather than a checkpoint is the cheapest instance of this folder's goal, and this paper shows the two things that make it hard to trust: all three baselines are identically zero, and the prediction is a best-of-sweep.** Keyword screening, a GPT-4o semantic judge *explicitly told that subliminal transfer exists and which surface indicators to look for*, and random injection return 0.00% on every cell of Table 1, so the positive result is a null-versus-something comparison — the same defect as a localisation method measured against freezing random components, one step earlier in the pipeline. Meanwhile α is swept and the best kept, non-monotonically (Table 5: 40.75, 43.25, 47.25, 0.50 across four consecutive values), so no number in the table is what a fixed procedure would have produced. The repair is one rung and is in the paper's own data: the Normal corpus is already a size- and style-matched control, so the honest statistic is the *difference* between the two signatures, which would also have explained the Reagan anomaly (98.40% actual against 22.00% predicted — right direction, magnitude off by 4×) instead of reporting it. For us: any corpus-level statistic gets a matched-corpus arm and a frozen-hyperparameter pass, because "beats a keyword list" is not evidence it reads the property. (arxiv-2602.04735, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2609.35261)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 178): **The corpus-level mean is a first-order summary, and its blind spot is the one every mean-difference read-out here shares — it cannot express that behaviour depends on dispersion, on a minority subset, or on order.** The whole dataset is compressed to one averaged final-token hidden state per layer, which is exactly why four instances suffice (a mean converges fast) and exactly why the method is blind to *which* four — the paper's own deferred task, instance-level attribution, is the question an auditor actually needs answered, and the mixture case is conceded harder without being run. The same limitation appears in this folder's decision benchmark, where ranking by mask averages picks the lowest-loss mask in only 3 of 30 cells because the dispersion term is invisible to the mean, and in its steering-vector entries, whose contrasts are means by construction. Transferable statement: a mean-of-representations read-out is a claim about the first moment and should ship with the second beside it (spread of per-instance cosine to the mean), because a corpus that is 1% toxic and one that is uniformly mildly toxic share a mean and have very different behaviour, and only the dispersion number separates them. (arxiv-2602.04735, arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2608.24037)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 177): **A predictor whose input is computed before the outcome it predicts is a categorically stronger claim than one fitted to post-hoc measurements, and the honest way to report it is a chain decomposition that scores each rung separately — this is the folder's first entry where the data-side link was shown to cost literally nothing.** The chain is D (bigram conditional entropy, from raw tokens, no training) → S (retained structure) → λ² (Weibull scale growth, from the weights), and the full-chain error equals the training-side-only rung to three decimals, so the entire error budget (5.7% RMSE, worst point 12.6% at the clean end) sits in the one linear-in-S fit and none in the inversion. Every other predictor in this folder — probes, attention statistics, hyperparameter regressions, meta-model readouts — is fitted against a quantity measured in the same run, so its error is an undifferentiated total. For us the adoption is a reporting shape: any forward predictor we build should be written as an explicit multi-rung chain with a per-rung error, because the rung that costs nothing is evidence the intermediate variable is real, and the rung that carries the error tells you which part of the model to fix. (arxiv-2608.23573, arxiv-2507.06445, arxiv-2609.03026)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 177): **A statistic that looks like it measures structure will also respond to a cheaper kind of structure, and the paper that finds this marks the boundary instead of fitting through it — code has *low* bigram entropy yet grows its weight scale the least, so the law's own variable is conflated and the boundary is quantified rather than asserted.** Over-prediction on the held-out code corpus is 0.50 in magnitude, about 6× the leave-one-out error, and the obvious repair is explicitly tested and ruled out: renormalising by a per-corpus shuffle ceiling does not help because the plug-in ceiling is ≈8.0 for every corpus at a fixed token budget, so the failure is not a baseline-choice artefact. The folder's counterpart is the scene where a feature dictionary scores equally on a randomly initialised model, and its probes whose matched-random arm flattens a localisation claim: a scalar read-out is only as good as the number of distinct causes it can be moved by, and one axis is one axis. The transferable discipline is to carry the off-law case into the report as a *quantified* margin, since that margin is the estimate of what the neglected second axis is worth — here redundancy, which the author then shows varies independently via a repetition sweep (growth peaking near eight-fold repetition, falling below baseline by thirty-two-fold, single seed). (arxiv-2608.23573, arxiv-2609.15533, arxiv-2605.06076)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 177): **State every weight-side claim in an additive currency and check additivity before aggregating, and use a through-origin refit to prove a fitted intercept is real — two cheap conventions no entry in this folder applies.** The law is written in λ² − λ₀² rather than λ because second moments pool across blocks and scales do not: the pooled coefficient matches the parameter-count-weighted average of the eighteen per-block slopes to 10⁻¹⁵, while an unweighted average gives 0.63 and a sum gives a meaningless 15.1 against a fitted 0.71. Separately, the non-zero injection floor is not assumed — a through-origin refit gives R² = −1.9, which is the two-line demonstration that the intercept is not a fitting artefact. Both habits apply directly to any per-layer or per-component statistic we report: check whether the quantity is additive under the pooling we perform (a variance-like statistic usually is, a normalised one usually is not), and when a model contains a baseline term, show that dropping it makes the fit worse rather than asserting it. Read against the folder's two-denominator rule, this is the same demand one level down — before comparing two aggregated numbers, establish that the aggregation you used is the arithmetic one the underlying unit admits. (arxiv-2608.23573, arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2603.30002)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 176): **The baseline that humiliates the internals is a hyperparameter list, and it only humiliates them because of how the split was drawn — the folder's sharpest instance of an eval-protocol artefact posing as a null result, and it cuts both ways.** Predicting from ID information alone whether a held-out model follows the hierarchical rule: on random 150/120 model splits the hyperparameter logistic regression beats both the head rule (0.85) and the five attention statistics (0.88); hold one (depth, weight decay) setting out entirely and hyperparameters collapse to chance (0.54) while both internals-based predictors keep their power. Nothing about the models changed, only whether test models shared a setting with training models. The lesson covers every "internals beat a simple baseline" claim in this folder and in our own work: a random split lets a structural predictor memorise the configuration, and the setting-held-out split is the only one that asks the question. The companion is the reporting order — the paper prints the unfavourable number in a table and then argues from the other split, rather than quietly dropping the first. (arxiv-2507.06445, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2506.02945)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 176): **A correlate can be anti-causal and still predictive, and the column that proves it is the one most intervention tables in this folder omit: in-distribution performance.** Uniform attention ablation improves OOD accuracy in models carrying sign-matching heads and degrades it in models carrying violation-detecting heads, though both subtypes correlate with the hierarchical rule at similar strength; the same ablation moves ID validation accuracy by 0.6% on average (median 10/1000, maximum 77/1000) and per-model ID and OOD effects are only weakly correlated. The field's standard faithfulness test — ablate, watch ID performance fall — was silent about a mechanism that is decisive on the edge cases, which the authors read as redundant backup circuits absorbing the damage in distribution. Read beside the localisation entry whose method was indistinguishable from freezing random components, and the actionability paper's demand for a collateral-damage column, the reporting rule for us becomes a 2×2 on every intervention: target behaviour ID and OOD, with and without it. A null on the ID diagonal is not evidence of irrelevance. (arxiv-2507.06445, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2605.11161)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 176): **The deliverable can be a prediction with no mechanism attached, and its cheapest form — a hand-written feature plus a random forest — is also the form most likely to be predictive across a population and least likely to survive a single model.** Five readout-position attention statistics (centre of mass, mass on the last tenth of the sequence, largest weight, weight on the readout token, mean self-attention, summarised over heads) reach 0.88 AUROC for the OOD rule and 0.72 on transfer to a second task family, beating the hand-named head rule and travelling between settings. That is the shape our predictors should take first, before anything involving a dictionary or a circuit: a named, computable, falsifiable statistic, scored on held-out models and on a held-out setting, with the mechanism question left open. The caution travels with it — a plurality of runs here differ by at least 10 OOD-accuracy points across seeds and the extreme gap exceeds 90 points, so a population-level predictor is predicting a distribution of training runs, not the model in front of you. (arxiv-2507.06445, arxiv-2605.01555, arxiv-2506.02945)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 175): **Price the readout against "something was mounted", not against "nothing was mounted" — the same-type-mismatched arm is the rung that turns a big number into a small one, and this paper is the cleanest instance because it prints all three cells.** Matching delta 0.2227 nats/token over no-update, mismatched-in-kind delta still 0.0972, so the item-specific information is the 0.1255 difference and the bulk of the apparent signal is the presence of a structured perturbation. Every read-out in this folder needs that middle rung in its units — the direction that beats its matched-random control, the probe that beats a same-size random subspace, the description that beats a shuffled-target description — and the arithmetic to report is a decomposition, not a gap: how much of the gain survives when the object is wrong but the format is right. For us the operative version is a pre-flight on any new predictor: build the wrong-object-wrong-in-format ladder before tuning the predictor, because the number that survives the middle rung is the only one we can defend when someone asks what our instrument sees that a structural null does not. (arxiv-2609.35261, arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2506.02945)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 175): **Abstention should be a trained output class, not a post-hoc threshold, and the cheapest way to train it is to put the null and the noise into the batch — here 8 no-change and 8 random-perturbation episodes ride alongside 24 real ones in every batch of 64, with their loss weights ramped in over the first 1,432 steps.** Read beside this folder's runtime-abstention certificate (a three-valued certificate over resampled datasets, where the abstained set was the finding) and its selection-filter lessons, the two implementations of the same idea are complementary: certify at inference when the method is a wrapper, but when the instrument is a *trained* reader, bake the refusal into training so the model has a state that means "this input carries no recoverable semantics". The ramp matters and is rarely reported: controls are introduced gradually so the reader does not spend its early capacity on the easy constant answer, which is also why the control losses here fall fast and the real losses fall slowly — a curve shape worth reading as a sign that the easy class was not allowed to dominate. (arxiv-2609.35261, arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2606.06267)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 175): **A description is not just a claim, it is a wide seed for an intervention, and the gradient trick that makes it one is refusing a second model — which reframes what "the reader works" means.** The Readout gets 2% Pass@100 on knowledge yet its target-likelihood gradient, transferred to the parent because the two share coordinates, moves three separate downstream measurements (refusal rate under two opposite targets, reasoning-trace form, BFCL Overall). That is this folder's predict-versus-act rule arriving from the weight side: the generation rate is a description-faithfulness number and the gradient arms are an action number, and they disagree by all of one to two orders of magnitude. It also carries the honest baseline this folder keeps asking for — the *same procedure with base-model gradients* fails to separate the two targets, which isolates the trained Reader's contribution from the pruning heuristic it is dressed as, and it makes the reading available: the readout's value is that it knows which rows to touch, not that it can say what it touched. - Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 174): **A stacked pass/fail predicate tree is the cheapest diagnostic format this folder has seen, because its failures are typed — R1 failing says the model ignores the input feature, R2 says the computation is not localised, R3 says it is not reused — and a scalar score cannot express any of those three.** The whole framework is thresholded per-example arithmetic on numbers an ordinary patching pipeline already produces: a clean-versus-corrupted logit gap, patched recovery as a fraction of that gap capped at one, and membership in the modal recovered-layer set, with each rule conditioned on its predecessors so the output is a three-deep tree rather than three independent scores. The substantive finding is that the same evidence supports a comparison the accuracy table cannot make (76% against 59% pass rate for schema-informed versus schema-free training, whose field accuracy differs by 5 points), and the layer result is the kind a scoreboard never shows: passing examples concentrate in layers 0–2 at 89% while the untrained baseline spreads across layers with 34% modal usage. For us the adoption is direct and cheap — any prediction our white-box model emits can be written as a small ordered set of predicates over the same intervention measurements, each with a named failure mode — and the caveat is the same one this folder's other certificates carry: the boundaries here are validation patches *inside* the schema token, so the tree is measured in a one-effect space and says nothing about whether the recovered layer is the mechanism or the most convenient site to patch. (arxiv-2603.23517, arxiv-2605.24033, arxiv-2602.16823)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 174): **The two-model comparison here is a deliberately crippled baseline, not a strong competitor, so the 17-point separation shows the rules detect a missing input feature — the easy end — and the paper's own broken contrast is what reveals it.** One model never sees the schema at training time, so the difference between the arms is not a difference in mechanism quality but a difference in whether the relevant information was ever available; a rule set that could not separate them would be worthless, and separating them costs nothing in specificity. The tell is the accuracy table: the no-schema model collapses to 0.0% exact match when a schema appears at test time and the schema model collapses to 10.4% when it is removed, so both arms are brittle to a distribution shift and the "genuine algorithm" arm is one condition away from the same failure. Read against this folder's dominated-baseline lesson (a localisation method indistinguishable from freezing random components) and its stronger negative-control designs (matched versus mismatched versus random, three rungs), the missing arm here is obvious and one training run away: a model trained with schema but with the schema *shuffled per example*, which would satisfy every rule's surface conditions while destroying grounding — and would test whether the predicates measure grounding or the mere presence of the token. (arxiv-2603.23517, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2607.18921)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 174): **"Invisible to accuracy" claims are themselves accuracy-cell choices, and the three position papers this folder now holds all make the same move — quote the cell that flatters the argument.** Here the headline contrast is a field-name accuracy of 93.5% for a model with schema withheld set against a 99.1% for a model with schema present, plus an exact-match cell at 10.4% that belongs to a test-time condition neither model was trained under; the number of accuracy points that genuinely separate the two arms under matched conditions is small, and the pass-rate gap is large, but the two quantities are computed over different example sets (the full test split versus 100 constructed pairs) so they are not a head-to-head. Compare the actionability position paper, whose figures are all borrowed from cited studies and inherit their setups, and the certified-circuit paper quoting two different accuracy/size pairings in its own abstract and introduction. The general rule for us is a reporting one: when we claim a method sees something accuracy misses, the accuracy we benchmark against must be computed on the same examples, under the same condition, with the same budget, or the claim is about our choice of baseline rather than about our instrument. (arxiv-2603.23517, arxiv-2605.11161, arxiv-2602.22968)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 173): **Stability can be purchased instead of measured, and the wrapper that buys it is a vote over resampled inputs rather than a better estimator — this is the first circuit entry in the folder whose output carries a radius instead of a percentage.** Every stability claim held here (cross-seed agreement, bootstrap resamples, paraphrase sets scored on average, subset-variation Jaccard) is an empirical frequency with no threat model attached; this paper runs the base algorithm on 100 random deletions of the concept dataset, thresholds the per-channel evidence, and gets invariance for *every* dataset within 5 edits at a stated confidence, abstaining where the evidence does not support a decision. The transferable instrument is the three-valued output plus its certification rate: the compactness gain here is partly abstention doing the work, and a reader shown only peak cACC cannot tell an accurate circuit from a smaller one. Read against the interpretive-equivalence and extraction-sensitivity entries, the general rule is that a robust claim needs a *radius* and an *abstention set*, and the abstained components — whose membership depends on which examples you looked at — are the finding rather than the error bar. (arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2603.30002, arxiv-2607.18921)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 173): **The measured quantity and the claimed one have different denominators on purpose here — a stability certificate is silent about coverage, and the paper's sufficiency defence is a full-model pruning accuracy that a stable-but-empty circuit would also pass.** The certified object is "these decisions will not change under bounded edits", which says nothing about whether the resulting subgraph carries the computation; that second claim is argued from cACC on the pruned model, and the two are reported side by side without being linked. Set beside this folder's reconstruction-beside-coverage pairs, its Jaccard-beside-nothing certificates and its faithfulness-beside-stability results, the pattern is now uniform enough to state as a requirement: when a method's headline is a guarantee, the guarantee needs its own certificate AND the same table needs a coverage number from an independent instrument, because every guarantee in this folder is one half of a two-number claim. The compensating evidence here is genuinely two-sided — other-class accuracy falling to 1% is a coverage-flavoured check the baselines fail — which is what makes the omission visible rather than fatal. (arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2609.15533, arxiv-2605.06076)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 173): **Abstention is a form of sparsity that no top-k baseline can express, and the ablation this paper does not run is the one that separates "the unstable channels are spurious" from "the unstable channels were never reliably estimable" — its own two different headline pairings are the tell.** The gain is attributed to unstable neurons being both unnecessary and harmful, but the same reduction would appear if the base algorithm's per-channel scores were simply noisy on a 100-image concept set, in which case the abstract's unexplained confound (it never ran the same top-k on a *larger* dataset) is the right control and is absent. Practical import for us: whenever a pruning or selection rule wins by dropping components, publish an arm that keeps the budget fixed and a noisier estimate of the same scores, because "certification found the spurious ones" and "certification filtered the noise" produce identical accuracy curves and call for different conclusions. The companion habit is scaled-down honesty: this paper quotes 91%/45% in the abstract and 56%/80% in the intro for the same result, so a reader who wants to compare it with another entry has to go to the table. (arxiv-2602.22968, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2607.18921)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 172): **"Same mechanism" is a set-valued property, and the cleanest way to claim it is a distance between implementation families rather than an agreement between two hand-picked graphs — this paper is the formal counterpart of the empirical result read beside it.** Interpretive equivalence is defined as the Hausdorff distance between the sets of models implementing each interpretation, estimated without ever writing an interpretation down by testing whether a model is closer to its own intervention-derived variant than to another model; the toy calibration shows the resulting score is graded rather than binary (0.43 within the four sorting interpretations, 0.01 across to the counting pair) and the applied arms recover the literature's own verdicts (Pythia within-family congruity 0.73 and 0.92 against 0.13 cross-family). Read with the extraction-sensitivity entry's finding that exact-edge overlap between two checkpoints is at chance on the near-miss split while the attention-head set is far above its baseline, the general claim is that every entry in this folder that compares extracted objects across checkpoints, seeds or training stages — and there are dozens — is publishing a point estimate of a set-valued quantity, and the two numbers it should publish instead are a diameter and a distance. (arxiv-2603.30002, arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2606.06267)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 172): **The correct negative control has three levels, not two, and the middle one is where the interesting finding lives — matched beats mismatched beats random, and the mismatched-above-random gap is the shared-task-cue confound in the same table.** Keeping the *matched* atomic circuits retains 0.920–0.926 of target predictions after ablation for the core circuit, keeping a *mismatched* low-overlap atomic union from the same checkpoint retains 0.722–0.774, and keeping size-, layer- and family-matched random components retains 0.298–0.332. The paper reads both gaps honestly: the matched-versus-mismatched gap says the correct source matters, and mismatched-versus-random says format and task-family cues contribute. That is the shape this folder keeps approximating and rarely prints: its matched-random arms (freezing arbitrary components, random top-k draws, shuffled-label probes) collapse the middle rung, so a positive result cannot be decomposed into "the mechanism" versus "the task's surface statistics". For us the import is a three-rung ladder in every control table, and a one-line statement of what the middle rung is expected to absorb. (arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2606.06267)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 172): **An "inert methodological choice" is a reportable finding, and the tell that a stability claim is weak is that it is about agreement rather than coverage — here two extraction choices move no conclusion at all while the paper cannot say how much mechanism either reported object contains.** Making attention heads' query and key families explicit rather than merged changes selected-node fractions by at most 0.024 and leaves every ordering by graph size intact (3/3 across three objects, two training families, five sparsity levels, three seeds), and sweeping the pruning budget over 0.04–0.20 also leaves it intact with gaps at most 0.055 — the honest reading being that these choices are *near-inert for the claims made*, not that they are harmless in general. Set beside the genuinely level-dependent result in the same paper (exact edges at chance on the near-miss split, head sets far above baseline), the rule is that a choice's inertness has to be demonstrated per claim, because the same kind of granularity choice is decisive for one claim and immaterial for another. The gap at the top of it is the one this folder's stability entries share: interpretive compression is never estimated, so "our description is stable" and "our description covers the computation" remain separate questions. (arxiv-2607.18921, arxiv-2603.30002, arxiv-2510.00845)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 170): **Score the decision, not the estimate — and this is the first entry in the folder that measures the gap on interpretable objects instead of arguing for it.** Mean-effect prediction improved from MAE 0.486 and 0.473 to 0.395 on held-out candidate masks and moved the fixed-action loss by 0.10% and 2.34% with intervals crossing zero; retargeting the same 92-column basis at the realized action loss instead moved it 18.5%. The mechanism is exact arithmetic rather than a modelling subtlety: action loss equals the distance of the predicted mean from the target plus a nonnegative prompt-to-prompt dispersion term, so an observer that ranks masks by their averages is systematically selecting the ones whose averages hide the most variation — even perfect knowledge of each mask's test-set mean picks the lowest-loss mask in only 3 of 30 pool–target cells. For us this is the reporting requirement the actionability entry only insisted on: our predictor emits a number that a controller will use, so every claim ships the estimation score and the cost of the action its own rule selects, and a predictor whose accuracy rises while its action cost does not is not an improvement. (arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2605.11161, arxiv-2506.02945)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 170): **An intervention scorecard without an exact no-op cannot answer the only question that matters first, because no-op's loss is known by construction — and this paper's own sign change is the demonstration.** At a one-logit target the direct-loss observer beats not acting by 10.9%, and at a half-logit target it is 46.2% *worse* than not acting, because the exact no-op's loss is precisely the target value; the same selection rule is good and bad depending only on where the target sits. Read against the folder's dominated-baseline and matched-random lessons (a localisation method indistinguishable from freezing random components; a surrogate beating random edges only past 80% of the network), the rule generalises to a one-line pre-flight for any editing or steering claim of ours: measure the null action, report the intervention's margin over it, and name the target region where the null wins. (arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2608.03913)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 170): **What a linear read-out must get right is a subspace, not a state — adequacy for control is matching at the starting point and along the span of allowed edits, and everything orthogonal to that span is free.** Every probe result in this folder is scored over the whole activation space (held-out AUC, paraphrase stability over a full hull, top-k overlap across all features); here the reachable set is `h_0 + span(B)` and the requirement collapses to two conditions, so a wrong coefficient on a coordinate the controller cannot move is provably harmless. The paired finding is that this restricted object still predicts real behaviour through a learned nonlinear suffix (correlation 0.952, leave-one-seed-out MAE 0.063 against 0.302 for the bias-only model), which is the honest form of the local-linearity assumption this folder keeps invoking: the nonlinearity is 16.1% of output movement and the affine certificate is still the best predictor of final error. For us the practical import is a denominator change — a prediction about a steering edit is claimed over the edit span, and the collateral-movement column is what catches the rest. (arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2604.09839, arxiv-2608.03913)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 170): **Separation inside every group coexists with a broken global threshold, and the failure is invisible to pooled AUROC — a safety observer with AUROC 1.000 in all four operation–format subgroups allocated 63.2% of its interventions to seen-form deletes and 18.4% to the doubly held-out one, where it lost outright to a features-only baseline.** This is the folder's grouping lesson arriving with a budget attached: score scales shift between deployment groups even when within-group ranking is perfect, so one global cutoff silently converts a good ranker into a bad allocator. The same shape appears in the APPS panels, where separation survives in every source family (AUROC 0.956–0.991) and length quartile (0.974–0.988) yet a family's share of caught attacks ranges 0.36–2.38 times its population share. Two consequences for us: report per-group allocation next to any pooled discrimination number, and re-fit the threshold per deployment group rather than shipping one learned on a mixed distribution. (arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2608.24037, arxiv-2605.01555)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 170): **The best context in which to read a model's internals changes between checkpoints of the same family, so "where to probe" is a property of the checkpoint and the deployment regime, not of the architecture — neutral context won on Qwen2.5, verdict-adjacent context won on Gemma and decisively on Qwen3.5 (1.976 against 6.601 mean violations).** Set beside this folder's temporal-validity entry (attention circuits migrate roughly twice as far as MLP circuits under the same optimisation) and its static-localisation entry (localising components beat full fine-tuning and was indistinguishable from freezing random ones), the general statement is that a measurement site validated on one checkpoint carries no transfer claim. The companion warning is the sparse-feature one, and the paper is scrupulous about it: an official Qwen-Scope SAE probe trailed a dense residual under a *disclosed* base-versus-post-trained checkpoint mismatch, and the Qwen2.5 sparse readout kept 127 coefficients instead of 3,584 while missing more than twice as many attacks — so compression is neither a decision nor a licence to compare across checkpoints. (arxiv-2609.03026, arxiv-2605.06076, arxiv-2605.01555)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 169): **A claim should be published with its refutation in the output space, not with its confidence in the metadata — and this is the first entry in the folder where a failed explanation is a deliverable rather than a result.** Every prior certificate here answers "how strong is the guarantee I have"; this one answers "here is the proposition, and here is the input on which it is false", returning the triple proven / refuted-with-witness / unknown. The demonstration is as cheap as it is decisive: the quote circuit agrees with the surrogate on 100% of the fitting dataset *and* on 100% of the bounded abstract domain, and the solver still produces a three-token input where the program and the model disagree — so agreement level carries no information about the existence of a counterexample, which is exactly the distinction this folder's pooled scores smooth away. For us the adoption is a reporting format, not a method: every prediction our white-box model emits should name its domain, its projection, its ablation semantics and the property asserted, and be reported as proven / refuted-with-witness / out-of-domain, because a predictor that can only say "usually right" is not making a claim anyone can check. (arxiv-2605.24033, arxiv-2602.16823, arxiv-2609.35686)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 169): **You can buy verifiability with architecture, and the paper prints the price — +0.196 OpenWebText loss and +9.12 WikiText-103 perplexity for the full SMT-friendly stack, with the normalization swap carrying almost all of it, and the author's own comparison says removing LayerNorm from pretrained weights currently beats replacing it in training.** This is the folder's cost-metric lesson at the level of the model rather than the read-out: the interpretable-by-design entry cost nothing in loss because it was scored on its own scale (a small model, a small task), whereas here the same bet is priced at GPT-2-small scale and loses visibly. The transferable habit is to state the interpretability tax *and* the alternative you were priced against — here trained-replacement versus post-hoc removal — since the honest reading is not "verifiability is expensive" but "verifiability is currently cheaper to obtain after training than during it". Read with the prototype-LM entry, the general rule for us is that any design-time change we recommend reports its loss delta at a scale where the baseline is strong, because a stack that trains stably is not the same claim as a stack that trains competitively. (arxiv-2605.24033, arxiv-2607.00510, arxiv-2605.11161)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 169): **A guarantee that passes through a surrogate should be published as a chain of named links, and the paper's own honest move is to say which link is the weak one — circuit fidelity to the model, surrogate fidelity to the circuit, program equivalence to the surrogate, with the symbol, the projection and the domain held fixed across all three.** This is the folder's two-denominator rule extended to three, and it differs from an averaged score in a way that matters practically: the middle link's strength is set by whether its validation was exhaustive over the domain or sampled, so the same top-line "verified" can mean two very different things and the entry can be compared with others only if that is stated. The same defect appears in this folder's judge pipeline (a description validated against a surrogate judge), in its paraphrased-input evaluations (a read-out validated against one rewrite model), and in its attribution proxies (an effect estimate validated against a first-order expansion), so the requirement generalises beyond verification: whenever our predictor's claim is checked through an intermediate object, the intermediate gets its own fidelity number and its own control. (arxiv-2605.24033, arxiv-2606.09899, arxiv-2506.02945)

- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 168): **A linear read-out over a frozen representation is not competing with the generative model that produced it — it is competing with that model's *own report*, and this is the first entry in the folder that scores a probe against that baseline rather than against chance.** Every read-out we hold is validated against a random or shuffled or orthogonal control; here the comparator is the judge's own numeric score, embedded into the model as a bias term so that the empty solution reproduces it exactly (`θ = 0 ⊕ 1, c = 0`), which turns "our probe works" into "our probe beats the model's introspection at a cost the model cannot match" — 4,096 parameters instead of billions, 0.775 GPU-minutes instead of 14.16 on the same data. That is the strongest form of the folder's recurring dominated-baseline argument, and it is what a *predictive* white-box model actually needs to show: not that a direction encodes the quantity, but that reading it is cheaper and more accurate than asking. The anchor construction is the cheap part worth stealing outright — every predictor we fit on top of an existing scorer should be parametrised so the zero-weight solution is that scorer, which makes the reported delta a delta and makes "never worse than the baseline" true by construction rather than by luck. (arxiv-2506.02945, arxiv-2605.11161, goodfire-com-research-reasoning-theater)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 168): **Fitting the level of a quantity and fitting its order are separate jobs, and optimising the first demonstrably destroys the second on the same rows — MSE halved while Kendall τ fell 0.272 → 0.214, and the fine-tuned baseline that nobody claimed was calibrated scores *better* on all three correlations.** This is the folder's two-denominator rule in its most mechanical form, because the two numbers are computed from one fitted model on one test set with no selection or filtering between them: the improvement is real on the metric the loss names, and the regression is real on the metric users of a ranker care about. The practical import is a reporting requirement, not a modelling one — any claim that our predictor "matches" a target publishes the fit statistic and the ranking statistic side by side, and says which one the loss optimised — and the companion observation is that accuracy and correlation do not co-move among the four judges here either (the multinomial judge wins exact accuracy on both rating datasets while losing Pearson r on the second), so a single headline number would have hidden the entire structure of the result. (arxiv-2506.02945, arxiv-2609.15533, arxiv-2603.01437)
- Pattern 2026-11-15 (run 168): **The strongest arm is the one where the cheap method loses, and here the authors print it — with abundant labels the fine-tuned judge wins outright on the largest preference dataset, and the read-out's advantage is confined to the small-label regime their ablations actually show.** The claim being defended is statistical efficiency, and the paper defends it the way the folder's better entries do: by naming the condition under which the advantage is a *parameter-count* fact (4,096 versus billions) and showing the crossover rather than averaging over it, with SFT ahead at all training sizes under Prometheus on accuracy and ahead up to 20% of data only for the other base judge. Read against this folder's cost-metric and matched-budget entries, the rule generalises to a one-line pre-flight for any "cheaper model is competitive" claim of ours: state the regime where the expensive arm wins, and if there is none, suspect the budget was never matched. (arxiv-2506.02945, arxiv-2605.01555, arxiv-2602.16823)
