The same audit applies to any grouping of ours that produces a readable label.
- **The binding constraint on a white-box model can be the tap, not the theory — so budget for the collection pipeline and publish its fidelity number**: a trillion-parameter model's SAE needs billions of tokens of activations, and the post's whole content is that getting them takes an inference-engine fork rather than an interpretability idea; the same asymmetry will hold for us, where a predictive model needs far more activations than a descriptive one. The transferable rule is the split they find: skip the phase of the forward pass your analysis does not need (prefill, if you are training a dictionary over collected text), capture where the shards are already merged, and push only handles and metadata across the host boundary. The habit that is *missing* and that we should not copy is the unverified tap — a throughput figure with no residual reconstruction error against a reference forward pass is a claim about a pipeline, not about the activations it produced, and one forward pass buys the difference. (goodfire-com-blog-interpretability-infra-at-frontier-scale, anthropic-com-research-engineering-challenges-interpretability, transformer-circuits-pub-2021-garcon-index-html)
- **Freeze provenance at the instrument boundary, because the instrument's batching is not an interface**: continuous batching flattens unrelated sequences into one token tensor, chunked prefill splits one document across several captures, tensor parallelism shards each activation across ranks, and the server's own metadata fields change meaning between modes — none of which is stable, documented API, so any downstream job written against them breaks on a version bump. Their writer does the right thing by reconstructing a canonical per-sequence record with absolute offsets and hiding the engine entirely from consumers, and the general form for us is that every probe, dictionary and attribution pass should consume an artifact whose schema we own, produced by one adapter per instrument. The corollary is a test we owe and they do not run: count the rows whose provenance fails to round-trip back to the source token, because a mis-joined activation is silently wrong rather than loudly broken, and every downstream number inherits the error. (goodfire-com-blog-interpretability-infra-at-frontier-scale, anthropic-com-research-engineering-challenges-interpretability, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-april-update-index-html)
- **Reaching the input path is what makes an intervention a different kind of evidence, so treat "we can write, not just read" as the milestone and say what it licensed**: the same hooks that let them read the residual also let them modify it, which is why real-time steering of a reasoning trace came almost immediately — and the emphasis they place on steering *chain-of-thought* is the right emphasis, since a prompt changes outputs while an internal edit changes the reasoning that produces them. The measurement gap is that the post claims the capability and shows a demo, so the reader cannot tell a working control loop from a working write path; the rule to import is that a reading pipeline and a writing pipeline differ only in which end of the same buffer you touch, and the moment you can write you owe the closed-loop evidence (dose-matched control, degradation branch, held-out scoring) rather than a before/after example. (goodfire-com-blog-interpretability-infra-at-frontier-scale, arxiv-2609.34056, goodfire-com-research-reward-hacking-activation-monitors)

## Patterns (mechanistic shaping)

- **Training against a read-out does not delete the concept, it relocates it — so every read-out we ship needs a stated recovery ladder, not just a score**: the mechanistic-shaping experiments put pressure on a concept direction and the model answers by regrowing the concept immediately through the task gradient, then re-encoding it (linearly at first, nonlinearly under frequent refitting, mid-training a second-order product code that is invisible to linear probes by construction), or relocating it to another layer. The instrument to steal is the five-level hierarchy — reuse / linear refit / nonlinear refit / different layer / black-box judge — because it converts "our probe broke" from a failure into a located fact, and it is cheap: five probe fits, not five experiments. Two habits follow directly: refit the read-out on a schedule in *any* setting where our measurement could interact with training (our own shaping, ablation, or fine-tuning arms), and never report a post-intervention read-out without the retrained-probe number beside it, since the original-probe score alone understates a concept that regenerated somewhere else. (goodfire-com-research-mechanistic-shaping, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-selective-gradient-masking, transformer-circuits-pub-2025-november-update-index-html)
- **"Do less training" is the reference line any training-time interpretability claim has to beat, and most methods merely slide along it**: on one capability-vs-sycophancy plane the post places data filtering, reward shaping, inoculation prompting, preventative steering along the same direction, and reduced-learning-rate DPO, and the spreading is the result — filtering only trades one axis for the other, the behavioural methods barely move sycophancy, and steering along the *same* direction as the shaping loss gets partway, which is itself evidence that the direction is the right handle. For our write-ups this is a reusable baseline ladder with a free null built in: whenever we claim an internal signal improved a behaviour, plot it against the same intervention with the signal's strength turned down, and report whether we are below the line or on it. The companion control from the reward-hacking arm is sharper still — filtered rollouts prevented cheating in only a third of runs while a penalty on the concept generalised to a task with a different forbidden file — so a behavioural filter is the wrong comparison when the behaviour has a common cause. (goodfire-com-research-mechanistic-shaping, anthropic-com-research-persona-selection-model, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-auditing-mo-replication)
- **Separate whether the model *uses* a concept from whether the concept is *present*, because only the second is what a text-level monitor can see**: reliance shaping (penalise attribution through the direction) and expression shaping (penalise the concept's presence along it) are two different losses for the same direction, and the paper needs both because the settings differ — a shortcut used to decide needs a reliance penalty, a behaviour to be suppressed needs an expression penalty. This is the cleanest available vocabulary for a distinction our survey keeps blurring, and it maps onto our own reporting: a probe's accuracy is an expression-side claim unless we have shown the direction is routed into the decision, and the cheap route to the routing half is the virtual-weight × coactivation downstream set the folder's circuit-tracing entries already use. Import both labels into our notes, and when we only have the presence measurement, say so instead of letting "we found the feature for X" imply use. (goodfire-com-research-mechanistic-shaping, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html, arxiv-2609.34056)

## Patterns (SAEs vs neural geometry)

- **Low reconstruction error is not evidence of a coherent explanation, and the diagnostic is a curve not a number**: a dictionary can reconstruct a curved concept perfectly while fragmenting it across dozens of redundant local detectors, so "high variance explained" is compatible with no interpretable structure at all. The cheap, architecture-agnostic test is to ask how reconstruction improves as you allow more atoms — if the curve keeps climbing well past the concept's intrinsic dimension instead of plateauing, the read-out is diluted and any single named direction for that concept is one tile of a mosaic. We should report that curve beside every directional claim, because it converts "our dictionary covers this behaviour" into a checkable statement about support size rather than a statement about the residual. (goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-august-update-index-html, anthropic-com-research-evaluating-feature-steering)
- **Group by function, not by direction: two nearly orthogonal directions can belong to one concept and two similar ones can belong to different concepts**: the manifold paper's comparison of five affinity metrics is the cleanest demonstration in the folder that decoder cosine similarity is the intuitive choice and the wrong one — cosine and magnitude correlation both fail to recover the known grouping while conditional co-activation and Ising couplings succeed. The reason is structural: under compact capture the spanning atoms are near-orthogonal by construction, and under tiling adjacent-region atoms point wherever they like. For our probes the transferable rule is that a cluster of directions is a claim about *co-occurrence after conditioning on the rest*, which is one graphical-model fit away, and that any grouping we form from angle alone should be labelled a geometric hypothesis that still owes the functional test. (goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html, goodfire-com-research-painting-with-concepts)
- **The stable object across independently trained instruments is the geometry, not the features — which gives us a free invariance test**: different SAEs barely agree on their atoms or on codes for random inputs, yet agree strongly on the coordinate system they induce *within one concept's manifold*. That asymmetry is worth more than any single accuracy number, because it says what a replication should compare. Fit our read-out twice — different seed, different dictionary recipe — and report both the atom-level disagreement and the geometry-level agreement; a read-out whose geometry is stable while its atoms are not is a read-out we can defend, and one whose geometry moves when the seed does is a measurement of the training run. The same logic justifies scoring concept-level predictions rather than feature-level identity whenever we compare against someone else's dictionary. (goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-auditing-mo-replication, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html)
- **Causal checks on a continuous variable should be tested along a path, not at a point**: interpolating between the centroids of successive bins of a concept and requiring diagnostic-token probabilities to order smoothly is a strictly stronger test than adding one steering vector and reading the sign, because it exercises the geometry the claim is about and catches a read-out that is merely correlated with the variable's extremes. The prediction we publish for such a variable should therefore be the whole curve across the range, with its expected ordering, not a single dose-response point — and the same shape applies to our own interventions wherever the underlying factor is continuous rather than binary. (goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, goodfire-com-research-self-correcting-search, arxiv-2312.06681)

## Patterns (model diff amplification)

- **The cheapest causal handle on a training run is the difference between two checkpoints, and it needs no dictionary at all**: LDA compares the pre- and post-update logits on the same context and amplifies their difference, which attributes the *change* to the update without ever asking which internal feature carries it — one forward pass per model, no labels, no probe fit. That is a different question from the feature-level ones this folder mostly asks ("which direction carries this behaviour"), and our survey has been treating them as interchangeable. The transferable habit is to report both reports where we can: a mechanism claim about which direction mediates a behaviour, and an attribution claim about which part of the update installed it, because a direction can be a faithful mediator whose installation was diffuse across the whole fine-tune, and vice versa. (goodfire-com-research-model-diff-amplification, anthropic-com-research-studying-large-language-model-generalization-with-influence-functions, anthropic-com-research-persona-selection-model)
- **A rare behaviour is usually latent long before it is probable, so sensitivity and prevalence are separate measurements and only one of them is what deployment cares about**: the 5%-trained checkpoint refuses in every one of fifty thousand ordinary rollouts yet, amplified, complies one time in twenty-five — meaning the behaviour was already answerable from the weights at a stage where any sampling-based evaluation would have called the model clean. For us this is the clearest available statement of what a predictive white-box model is *for*: not to re-derive the base rate a sampler already gives you, but to say which rare behaviours the current state supports, and to say it at a point where sampling cannot. The practical import is that any evaluation whose only output is a rate is measuring the easy half, and any probe result stated as an accuracy is also measuring the easy half. (goodfire-com-research-model-diff-amplification, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-cheap-monitors, anthropic-com-research-probes-catch-sleeper-agents)
- **Third time in three entries: the coefficient of an added vector is meaningless without the norm of the thing it is added to**: α has to be chosen relative to the magnitude of the logit difference and shrunk as training proceeds (the difference grows), exactly as the steering-magnitude bookkeeping demanded a perturbation-to-residual-norm ratio and the transplant entry demanded a dose-matched constant-push control. Any intervention of the form "add a vector in this direction" — amplification, steering, transplant, ablation-by-projection — has a free scale parameter whose usable range is set by the state it is added to, so the standing rule for our write-ups is to publish the ratio, not the multiplier, and to name which way the ratio must move as the underlying quantity changes. (goodfire-com-research-model-diff-amplification, transformer-circuits-pub-2025-august-update-index-html, arxiv-2609.34056)

## Patterns (mixing mechanisms)

- **Build counterfactuals in which every competing hypothesis predicts a different observable, so one intervention adjudicates between them**: the binding paper's whole empirical design is four predictions from one swapped residual vector — positional, lexical, reflexive, and "no effect" matching the unintervened output — which is why a single patching run can rank three accounts instead of confirming one. Contrast this with the folder's more common pattern of patching one direction and reporting that behaviour moved, which cannot distinguish the hypothesis under test from any other thing that vector carries. The procedural rule worth adopting: before running an intervention, write out the prediction table for all live hypotheses including the null, and redesign the prompt pair until the columns disagree everywhere.
- **Score a predictive account against the guessing baseline, not against zero — and treat "below the baseline" as the interesting outcome**: Jensen–Shannon similarity runs in [0,1] with a uniform distribution sitting near 0.5, so the established positional account scoring 0.44–0.46 is not "a weak model" but a model that is anti-informative, worse than refusing to predict structure at all; this is the same lesson the folder's feature-identification entry taught about normalised-rank metrics, arriving from a different direction. The habit: state the indifference point of any bounded metric beside every score, and when a published account lands near or below it, say so in those words rather than reporting a percentage improvement over a rival that is itself broken.
- **A mixture with input-conditional weights is a legitimate white-box object, and it is small**: once the right terms were in the model — a Gaussian around the group index with width a quadratic in the normalised position, a one-hot at the lexical index, a one-hot at the reflexive index — six learned scalars reached 0.95 JSS against a 0.96–0.98 oracle, and the shape mattered more than the existence of the term (one-hot instead of Gaussian cost 0.10). For our own predictor the import is that the payoff is in naming the correct *functional form* of each mechanism and letting per-input weights interpolate, not in a bigger surrogate; and that the gap to the oracle is the honest measure of how much of the gap is parameterisation rather than mechanism.
- **The mechanism can change with an index the model computes, so pooled probe results average three mechanisms and describe none**: the same retrieval task is solved positionally at the ends of the list and lexically or reflexively in the middle, and which substitute appears depends on the target's slot within its clause — so a read-out fit over all conditions reports a mixture whose weights are an artefact of the data's condition distribution. This is the sharpest version yet of the folder's recurring warning about strata: before fitting a probe on a behaviour, identify the index that governs which mechanism is active, and report the read-out per stratum with the mixture weights, rather than one number over pooled cases.

## Patterns (geometry vs computation)

- **A well-shaped manifold in representation space does not tell you the computation, and the two tests that separate them are cheap**: the folder's turn to manifolds has been quietly assuming that if a concept sits on a circle, the mechanism rotates along it. Here it does not — Llama's months circle exists at the input token and at late layers, but the layer that combines input and offset has no circle at all, so the adding happens in a base-10 Fourier space and the concept circle is written *afterwards*. The transferable pair of measurements: (a) probe for the geometry at the *specific* layer and position where the causal variable gets consumed (not anywhere the circle is easy to find), and (b) check whether a *different* periodicity — one the concept does not have — predicts the output just as well. If the second one works better, the manifold is a read-out, not a basis. This is the same lesson the folder's exemplar-and-probe entries have been circling, arriving through geometry instead of features, and it should be a standing clause in any write-up that shows a manifold.
- **The cheapest real faithfulness test is cross-task transfer of a direction that was fit on a *different* task**: Fourier probes fit only on "a+b=" were then used to steer months, weekdays and hours, with no labels from those tasks, and they moved the answer to the target concept. A probe's in-distribution accuracy proves the information is linearly available; a probe fit elsewhere that still *causes* the behaviour proves the direction is the one the model uses. Whenever we have more than one task that shares a mechanism, this should replace the usual "probe accuracy on held-out examples" line, at the cost of one more training run.
- **"Zero everything except my set" is a stronger and more informative ablation than "zero my set"**: zeroing the 28 neurons kills accuracy, but the retain-only arm shows the set is nearly sufficient *and* localises what is missing — the residual error sits almost entirely at large summands, which is exactly where the hand-set threshold would have excluded the largest-period neurons. One extra arm turns an ablation into a map of your own theory's blind spot. Contrast with the folder's usual single-arm ablations, which report damage but cannot say whether the identified object is complete.
- **When accuracy falls with a magnitude, check whether the failing stage is downstream before calling the mechanism broken**: months accuracy runs 100% → 68.1% → 30.8% as the pre-modulo sum grows, and errors hug diagonals of the sum map; patching the same prompts into the addition task exposes the *correct* internal sum in 63% of them. So the arithmetic is right and the number→concept conversion degrades with magnitude. Regular, structured errors are evidence about which stage failed, and a two-task read-out is what converts "it gets harder" into a stage attribution.

## Patterns (explanatory variables vs descriptions)

- **An explanation that predicts a failure mode is stronger than one that describes a mechanism, and the price is that the mediating quantity is usually unobservable**: this paper's move is to make superposition an explanatory *variable* — sweep the sparsity that controls it, show the vulnerability multiple tracks it (r ≈ 0.99 in the appendix replication), then show that the intervention aimed at the failure (adversarial training) moves the geometry back. That ladder is worth copying wholesale, but notice what it costs: in ResNet18 the mediating quantity can only be reached through two SAE-derived proxies (reconstruction loss at fixed sparsity, and L0 of the code), and each proxy has a rival story. For our own work the import is a labelling discipline — every quantity in a causal claim gets tagged *intervention* or *proxy*, in the same sentence. (arxiv-2508.17456, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, arxiv-2609.34056)
- **Check whether the intervention is the objective before calling it a causal direction**: "adversarial training reduces superposition" is presented as the novel half of the result, but adversarial training minimises worst-case interference by construction and superposition is what interference *is*, so the finding is close to restating the loss. The informative arm is the reverse one, where an input-distribution parameter (sparsity) is moved and the failure follows. The habit worth importing: when a result says "training for X changed Y", ask whether X's loss already contains Y, and if it does, report the effect size only as a sanity check and put the weight on the direction the objective does not imply. (arxiv-2508.17456, arxiv-2507.16795, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-auditing-mo-replication)
- **Publish your errata where a reader will hit them, and treat a fixed figure as evidence about figures in general**: this paper carries a Revision History note saying a plotting bug in its Figure 6 code had been inflating the clean-versus-adversarial gap. Nothing in the extracted prose flags which sentences were written before the fix, and the numbers as read now agree with Table 2 — which is the point: a reader who only sees the repaired text cannot tell a figure-derived claim from a table-derived one. Two consequences for us: label every number taken from a plot, and prefer the table when a paper offers both. (arxiv-2508.17456, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-july-update-index-html, anthropic-com-research-evaluating-feature-steering)

## Patterns (weight-side vs activation-side explanations)

- **Four constraints that are each gameable and hard to satisfy together is a better standard than one strong metric**: VPD asks for exact reconstruction, rank-one simplicity, per-prompt minimality and behavioural fidelity in the same object, and it is the conjunction that carries the argument, not any single number — which matters because the document reports no numbers at all and is still persuasive. The transferable habit is to write our method descriptions as a list of independently falsifiable constraints and then report where each one is *only just* met, since a claim resting on one strong metric is a claim about that metric, while a claim resting on four weak ones is a claim about the object. (goodfire-com-research-vpd-explainer, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, arxiv-2609.34056)
- **Turn "which parts matter here" into a learned, attackable prediction rather than a selected set**: the causal-importance network makes per-prompt importance an object with its own accuracy, and the adversarial mask search then hunts for exactly the case where its claim of irrelevance fails — which is the same failure mode the folder's circuit entries keep tripping over when an importance-pruned subgraph looks faithful until someone stress-tests it. Any sparse account we publish should ship with the adversary that tries to break it, and with the honest question of whose error a false "irrelevant" label belongs to, because an auxiliary predictor trained jointly with the decomposition is a second model whose mistakes are indistinguishable from the decomposition's. (goodfire-com-research-vpd-explainer, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html, anthropic-com-research-open-source-circuit-tracing)
- **Activations say what the model is computing at a position; parameters say what it can compute at all — and the folder has been writing almost exclusively about the first**: the summary's framing is the cleanest statement of a gap in our own survey, since a probe reading a direction at one layer is by construction a statement about a state, while a piece of weights is a statement about capability that holds before any input arrives. The practical import is that a *predictive* white-box model must predict from both halves — the activation side gives the input-conditioned value, the weight side gives the repertoire — and any account that only has the first should say so when it claims to predict behaviour on inputs unlike those measured. (goodfire-com-research-vpd-explainer, arxiv-2511.05408, arxiv-2610.07334)
- **When an algorithm spans heads, the circuit's members are query/key pairs rather than heads, so any read-out that treats a head as a unit has assumed away the usual case**: previous-token behaviour and syntax-boundary routing both came back as distributed Q/K subcomponent pairs, with a footnote saying this is generally true — the same conclusion the folder's circuit entries reached from the activation side, arriving from the weights. For our reporting this means the unit of a mechanism claim should be named explicitly and defended, and that a head-level attribution is a *coarse-grained* claim whose refinement is a pair-level one, not a claim about a natural unit. (goodfire-com-research-vpd-explainer, transformer-circuits-pub-2025-november-update-index-html, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html)

Full text incl. Appendix A–G; no figure inspected. GPT-2 layer 7 main, 96 seeded TopK SAEs (k=64, F=2^14), 1B FineWeb tokens; unit = decoder vector. Stability = per-feature reappearance probability at argmax decoder cosine >= 0.7 over 95 sibling seeds (Hungarian check IoU 0.978 ± 0.001), endpoints at ε=0.05. Bimodal distribution, mean p ~0.75. Functional asymmetry: unstable features fire less (0.18% vs 0.44%) and hold far less reconstruction / next-token-loss mass under frequency-matched masking (N stable vs 4N unstable, 10 masks, norm-reweight arm); explanations split surface-form vs structural ("substring" 38.9% vs 11.3%, "phrase" 4.1% vs 32.0%), perfect detection scores 4.5x rarer for unstable, and GPT-5 classifies stability from explanation text alone at 0.88. Geometry: unstable sets are lower effective rank (ER/d 0.587–0.649 vs 0.804–0.808), linearly separable at F1 ~0.73 with cross-seed F1 ≈ within-seed, and their top-r subspace transfers across seeds, which the planted low-rank synthetic model reproduces (full-rank ~1.0 vs low-rank ~0.25 reappearance). Variants: vanilla 0.003 unstable at lower EV, HierTopK 0.028, JumpReLU 0.038, TopK≈BatchTopK; higher k buys EV and costs stability; instability plateaus ~8% at 10B tokens; Mahalanobis/whitening buys stability at EV cost; most-probable feature-pool construction recovers near-baseline EV with SAEBench AutoInterp 0.850 vs 0.818. Dead-salmon control: SAEs on random GPT-2 keep high detection scores while the stable fraction collapses. Limits they name: two arbitrary thresholds, one mechanism not the mechanism, no-trade-off scoped to pooling. Mine, marked: no matched-extra-budget baseline for pooling, seeds share data order so optimiser-variance instability is invisible, subspace transfer untested across width/style.

- **A read-out needs a reproducibility score, and the score has to be computed before any semantic claim is made**: reappearance probability across independently seeded reruns is the cheapest possible audit of a direction's existence — one feature, N sibling trainings, a cosine threshold — and it converts "we found the direction for X" into "the direction recurs in 94 of 95 reruns, and here is the rate for a direction we believe is noise". The measured structure in the seed-dependence paper is what makes the score interpretable rather than a bare number: irreproducible units are low-frequency, low-entropy surface-form triggers with little reconstruction mass, so a dictionary's unstable fraction is a measure of how much of it describes the tokeniser rather than the computation. Any entry in our model should ship with the rate, the threshold, and the resulting stable fraction, because a claim that cannot state its own reproducibility is a claim about one checkpoint.
  (arxiv-2606.12138, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html)
- **An interpretability score is not a reproducibility score, and the two can point in opposite directions — report both or neither**: SAEs trained on a randomly initialised transformer kept high auto-interpretation detection scores while their cross-seed stable fraction collapsed, which is the same failure the folder already records for features-as-classifiers (a legible descriptor sitting on a dataset artefact) and for rank metrics (a method barely above a free baseline). The procedural import is to pair every plausibility measurement with a null that should destroy it — random model, random directions, shuffled labels — and to treat the gap between the two as the object of interest rather than the headline number. This is also why a probe's held-out accuracy alone cannot license a mechanistic story: accuracy against a label is not evidence that the direction survives a rerun of the training.
  (arxiv-2606.12138, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html)
- **When individual units are seed-dependent but their span is not, the seed-invariant object is a subspace — so name the unit you claim and defend it**: unstable directions were non-identifiable one-to-one across seeds at cosine 0.7, yet one seed's top-r singular subspace explained the other seeds' unstable sets, and a planted low-rank block reproduced the effect from first principles. For a predictive white-box model this settles a reporting question the folder has circled since the geometry entry: a claim about "the direction for X" is a claim about a basis choice, the retrainable object is the subspace and the interactions inside it, and the honest form of a read-out is a span plus an argument that the span, not the basis, is what the model uses. It also explains why two dictionaries can both be right and neither be canonical, which reframes a null read-out as possibly a basis mismatch rather than an absent mechanism.
  (arxiv-2606.12138, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry, arxiv-2604.07615)

- **A cheap probe is a different claim from a good probe, and the control that proves it is a call-budget-matched one**: the deployment report's cleanest result is that sending probe-*selected* exchanges to a judge holds the judge's recall ceiling at about a sixth of the judge calls, while sending *randomly* selected exchanges loses recall roughly linearly — so the internal state is carrying something the turn-level text sampling cannot reach. That is a stronger form of "the probe does work" than any AUROC, because it isolates the information content from the model's competence, and it costs one extra arm to run. Adopt it as the default ablation for every monitor or cascade claim we make: hold the expensive step's budget fixed, compare internal-signal selection against random selection, and report the recall at the declared operating point rather than a threshold-free metric. The companion warning from the same report is that richer probe functions are not automatically better — linear probes gave up about 5% recall against their recipe, but nonlinear probes lost up to 30% on out-of-distribution sets, and a text n-gram baseline had to flag nearly every turn to reach the same point. (goodfire-com-research-production-cyber-monitors-on-kimi-k3, goodfire-com-blog-probe-monitors-101, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-cheap-monitors)
- **A session-level metric hides where in the trajectory the read-out starts working, and that is exactly the question a predictive model has to answer**: the cyber monitors are described as reading behaviours both confined to a chunk of a turn and persisting across it, and the architecture reflects that (multi-position read-out, custom kernels carrying scores through the cache), but nothing in the report separates the two — the headline number is per-session recall after aggregating over turns. For our purposes the informative experiment is the opposite direction: a per-position probe curve over a session whose intent escalates mid-way, asking whether the intent signal is present from the first token or appears at a single step, because a detector that fires late and one that fires early are different claims about the representation and only the early one supports acting before the tool call. Two lesser lessons sit alongside it: an end-to-end blocking rate that mixes monitor, judge and system prompt (29%→96%) must not be quoted as the probe's accuracy, and a 0% false-positive figure on traffic with no adversarially-framed benign requests is a lower bound. (goodfire-com-research-production-cyber-monitors-on-kimi-k3, anthropic-com-research-probes-catch-sleeper-agents, alignment-anthropic-com-2025-auditing-mo-replication)

If an edit changes behaviour on material the model could already produce, the honest description is a change of emphasis or selection; if a claim is that the model's *belief* moved, the evidence has to rule out the model simply expressing a pre-existing capability more readily, which means testing the edited model on held-out queries it has never been steered toward and on facts it could not have held. - **Score a dictionary by what an ablation of its latents does to other concepts, not by what it recovers**: the erasure paper's TPP score is the cheapest concept-specificity test in the folder — pick the latents a class probe attributes to, ablate them, and require the target probe to fall while the other class probes stay put — and its value is that the cross-probe asymmetry, not the drop itself, is the claim. Almost every "these features encode X" result in this folder reports only the drop. The companion measure is the skyline normalisation: accuracies are divided by the oracle probe's, so 0.4 of a possible increase means the same thing across concepts and models. (arxiv-2411.18895, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html, anthropic-com-research-evaluating-feature-steering)
- **A metric that lacks a shape prior will be solved by the degenerate case, so check unimodality and training-monotonicity before trusting it**: both new evaluations here are validated by two properties that cost one extra sweep — the score peaks at some intermediate sparsity rather than rising monotonically with density, and it improves across training checkpoints. The failure mode they catch is concrete: an untrained Standard SAE with L0 ≈ 9000 scores *well* on the judge-free metric, because a dense dictionary ablates well by brute force. Any of our own scores should be run against a random checkpoint and against density-matched ablations for exactly this reason. (arxiv-2411.18895, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-august-update-index-html, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html)
- **A probe's accuracy is a claim about what the probe found, so the correlated-signal setting needs the probe itself reported**: with a task that carries two correlated cues, the same recipe debiases in opposite directions on two models purely because the probe captured a different cue, and the probe's batch size and learning rate flip which one it is. The habit to import is one line in every result: which cue did the probe actually read, verified on the balanced set — because otherwise a downstream intervention that "removed the spurious feature" may have been removing the task feature. (arxiv-2411.18895, anthropic-com-research-probes-catch-sleeper-agents, arxiv-2511.00617)

- **A dictionary that several models share is a different object from a dictionary one model learned, and the test is adaptation onto a frozen space**: portability is the property our own read-outs should be measured on if they are to be a model of a network rather than a description of a checkpoint, and it is cheap to test — freeze the dictionary, train only the new model's in/out maps, then re-check every sharedness criterion and not just reconstruction. The numbers here say the property is real but not free: a post-trained sibling and an out-of-lab model both attach above 1.0 of their own dedicated SAE, while an architectural outlier attaches only when the training already made solo selection in-distribution. The transferable rule is that a read-out claim should name the models it was trained on and then show a cold-start attachment, because a dictionary refitted on each new model reproduces the original result without sharing anything. (arxiv-2609.04344, arxiv-2606.12138, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry)
- **Reconstruction quality is not evidence that a representation is shared, and the ablation that proves it is the one the loss cannot see**: normalising the vote before the shared selection versus not normalising leaves training loss flat and moves the per-model share of the dictionary from near-even to one model holding essentially all of it — the same shape as the folder's earlier finding that an interpretability score and a reproducibility score can disagree. Any multi-stream, multi-task or multi-layer representation claim we publish should carry one variant that the objective cannot distinguish and the property can, and report the property's number for both. The corollary for reporting is to prefer criteria the training loss does not directly optimise: selection agreement and magnitude agreement are both in the objective here, which is exactly why the authors put the weight of the argument on cold-start adaptation. (arxiv-2609.04344, arxiv-2411.18895, arxiv-2606.12138)
- **A label transferred across models is still a label, so the transfer table has to keep the faithfulness column separate**: cross-model clarity, responsiveness and purity correlate around 0.92 while faithfulness correlates at 0.371, and the authors read that gap — correctly — as semantic transfer without functional equivalence. The habit is structural: whenever a descriptor is evaluated by an LLM or a judge, the score decomposes into "does the label identify this thing" and "does the thing do what the label says", and only the second licenses any prediction; averaging them hides exactly the component our model needs. The same separation turns a null steering result into information, since detectors of a token never steer at any dose in any model, which is the input/output feature distinction measured rather than assumed. (arxiv-2609.04344, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-features-as-classifiers-index-html, anthropic-com-research-evaluating-feature-steering)

- **A rejection of a heuristic is only informative if the curves it replaces were measured under the same conditions as the curves that replace them**: this paper's headline is that injection at the probe-best layer is roughly 26× weaker than multi-layer injection in the mid-to-late band, but the two arms differ in layer *count* as well as layer *position*, and the paper's own four-condition table supplies the piece that makes the claim diagnostic — a single-layer injection at L18 reaches about 7× the single-layer probe-best effect, so position is doing most of the work. Two habits follow for any "our site is better than the obvious site" result: put the matched-count arm for the competing site in the main table and not in the discussion, and report the ablation of your own recipe (multi-layer vs single-layer, direction variant, dose) beside it, because otherwise the ratio you publish is a ratio of recipes and the reader cannot tell how much of it is the variable in the title. The second-order version of this is the paper's own honest failure: its two-factor predictor fits one model exactly, another to within a layer, and misses the third by nine layers, so a heuristic can be *directionally* right and *numerically* unreliable across architectures at once. - **Coverage, not similarity, is the number that licenses a transfer claim — and it is computable before you touch the target**: the paper's contribution is a label-free score ‖δ_S S_λ‖/‖δ_S‖ that says what share of a read-out the fitting data spans, and it behaves like a threshold (≥0.95 → ~99% recovery, <0.8 → ~4%). This is the same shape as the reproducibility and interpretability scores already in the folder, applied to a third axis: a direction can be legible, reproducible, and still be non-portable because the data behind the map never varied along it. Any white-box predictor we publish should carry all three, and the coverage one is the cheapest because it needs no target labels and reuses the eigendecomposition the fit already produced.

- **A read-out is a function of a context string, not of a topic, and topically-matched data will not cover it**: the general map contained 600 ARC questions and still recovered 16% of the ARC gain, because the correctness direction reads a question followed by a candidate answer while the map's data had questions alone; swapping in same-kind prompts from *other* datasets was enough (73–88%), and a GSM8K-only map transferred nothing because its prompts never vary along the refusal direction. The rule to import is that contrast directions should be fitted, and any surrogate that stands in for them evaluated, on the exact input format the read-out consumes — and that "we have data from this domain" is not the same claim as "our data covers this tool".

- **Portability is evidence that a mechanism corresponds, not that a read-out adds value — so test the two separately**: refusal transfer saves no labelling at all (the target's own direction from the same 16 prompts per class recovers 97%), while carried read-outs beat what the target's unlabelled representations yield (ARC ≈ 25 labelled questions; a probe carried through 10 unlabelled reviews beats one built from 10 labelled by 9 points). Carrying the split into our own write-ups: prove correspondence with a tool that can be rebuilt in the target, and prove usefulness with a tool whose labels the target does not have, and never present the first as the second.

- **Similarity, retrieval, and causal transfer are three different claims, and only the third is a transfer result**: this study has all three rungs on the same models and they narrow monotonically - alignment for every causal pair, projection well above chance for every causal pair, generation-level causal effect for one of three - and the killer cell is Mistral, which had the joint-strongest projection accuracy (50%) and a 0.0% causal effect against a 3.3% control. The reading we should import is structural rather than numerical: a hidden-state similarity score and a cross-model retrieval score are measurements of geometry, and neither licenses the sentence "model A's representation of X can stand in for model B's". For our own write-ups that means separating the three claims into three sentences with three different evidence types (cosine or kNN for similarity, held-out top-1 for correspondence, matched negative-control intervention for function), and never letting a strong first or second rung be reported as support for the third. (arxiv-2608.16347, arxiv-2611.12675, arxiv-2609.22135)

- **Run the random-initialisation null and one scale-invariant metric before believing any cross-model comparison**: the trained-versus-untrained check is what caught CKA and Procrustes ranking randomly initialised models as *more* aligned than trained ones (0.81-0.82 vs 0.013-0.015; 0.95 vs 0.11-0.12), and the cause they give - a few high-magnitude activation dimensions dominating kernel- and rotation-based scores - is the same failure this folder already knows from probing and from SAE decoder geometry. The habit is cheap and general: for any representational comparison across checkpoints, models or layers, report a null built by re-initialising the same architecture and report at least one rank-based, scale-invariant statistic beside the linear-kernel one. A metric that says noise aligns better than training is a defect in the metric, and finding that out after publication costs the whole result. The corollary is the SYNONYM control: swapping a topical pair set for a lexically disguised true-synonym set costs almost nothing and separates co-occurrence clustering from semantic alignment, and here it demoted three of four models. (arxiv-2608.16347, arxiv-2606.12138, arxiv-2411.18895)

NOT in SEED_QUEUE; taken from outside the queue as run 123's first candidate.

## Patterns (geometric vs causal equivalence)

- **A similarity score between two read-outs is a claim about coordinates, not function — so every cross-model or cross-checkpoint match needs a paired-intervention correlation beside it**: on 68 high-firing shared latents the median decoder cosine is 0.965 while the median correlation of ablation effects is 0.616, and the tails fail in both directions — decoders at cosine > 0.95 with *anti-correlated* downstream effects, decoders at cosine ≈ −0.50 with effects correlating near +0.91. The mismatch is the same failure this folder has now met four times from four directions (a legible feature that is causally idle, an interpretability score that a random checkpoint also earns, a cross-model retrieval score that predicts nothing about generation, a similarity metric that ranks untrained models above trained ones), and the cheapest repair is uniform across all of them: choose a unit, perturb it identically in both systems on the same inputs, correlate the effect profiles, and print that number next to the similarity number. The cost is one extra forward pass per unit per system, and it needs no retraining, which is what makes it a reporting rule rather than an experiment. (openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder, arxiv-2608.16347, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html)
- **A taxonomy boundary is not a functional boundary, and the control class is where that shows**: the latents the standard norm-based classification rejects as "not shared" still carry a latent whose cross-model ablation effects correlate at 0.999, while the class it *does* call shared runs at a median of 0.616 — so the label "shared", "exclusive" or "dead" is a statement about decoder norms and says nothing about transferability in either direction. The transferable habit is to sample the control class deliberately and report its *best* member rather than its mean, because a single counterexample inside the rejected class refutes the boundary as a decision rule, and a mean would have hidden it. The companion observation is architectural rather than specific to this pair: BatchTopK plus L1 drove the exclusive classes to essentially zero on this model pair where a vanilla-L1 recipe on the same pair reports a few percent, which is the folder's recurrent warning that the load-bearing number in any dictionary comparison may be the recipe rather than the finding. (openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder, arxiv-2609.04344, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry)

Pipeline: attribution graph on a **single** prompt ("The war lasted from the year 1711 to 17") with their own reimplementation of graph construction and pruning, no supernode clustering; features ranked by edge attribution to the top-10 logits, top 16 per logit = 160 candidates pre-deduplication; then the prior neuron-level logit-attribution analysis transferred to features — the activation-weighted **sum of a feature's decoder columns over all later layers** dotted with each candidate output-year unembedding, filling a years×years heatmap by re-running a **local replacement model** (base MLPs preserved, CLT reconstruction added) over ~100 prompts, one per input year. **Results:** the mechanism is recovered — weight concentrates from the masked year's final digit through middle-to-late layers to the prediction position, and the top features show the promote-above / suppress-below signature (425104 at layer 8 is the top input feature for one logit and fires before the largest year, including a Roman-numeral date; 407684 generalises to prices, percentages and measurements). Beyond the known circuit: a parity/opposition feature (399423) promoting even outputs after odd inputs and firing on "pros and cons" / "right or wrong", multiples-of-five and ends-in-1→2 structured-number features, and 402486 (rank 14 of 137 for its logit) implementing the inverse comparison while reading as a general small-number detector. **The published centre of gravity is a mismatch:** several top features' heatmaps barely vary with input year while their examples do (425104), 349410 shows the reverse, 461858 is a narrow band (inputs 6–14, outputs 10–30) and reads as a special-case lookup — so the recovered space is *less* clean than the neuron-level account, with no counterpart in the prior work for the structured-number family. Limits they name: the divergence is unexplained and attributed to logit attribution scoring features in isolation; attribution techniques were built for Transformers while a CLT feature writes to several layers, so their transfer is unproven; single selection prompt; position-to-position tracing — CLT's advertised advantage — untested because logit attribution needs final-position features. Mine, marked: no held-out task, no faithfulness metric, no ablation and no random-feature baseline (success = expert visual comparison with a figure from the earlier paper); "recovers the mechanism" rests on a hand-selected subset of 160 candidates with no count of the uninteresting remainder; the dictionary is the authors' own, so recipe differences from the original CLT paper are uncontrolled. NOT a uniform audit of the pipeline's failure rate — it is a curated walkthrough.

## Patterns (recovery drills and replacement-model fragmentation)

- **A recovery drill is the only interpretability evaluation that cannot be gamed by a pretty picture, and it has to publish the near-misses**: asking a pipeline to find a mechanism that independent work already established, from one prompt, and reporting the features that *disagree with their own examples* is what turned this entry from a demo into evidence — 425104 promotes years above ~12 and strongly above ~60 irrespective of input year while its max-activating examples track the largest year, so a report showing examples alone would have called it a clean greater-than unit. The transferable protocol for our own work is three lines on every recovered mechanism: the mechanism we expected (from prior work), the feature we found, and the measurement on which they disagree; and the count of candidate units examined so the reader can compute a hit rate. The corollary is that a mechanism with a *known* input-output signature is the right test bed, because the years-by-years heatmap is ground truth we did not produce. (goodfire-com-research-replicating-circuit-tracing-for-a-simple-mechanism, arxiv-2604.07615, transformer-circuits-pub-2025-november-update-index-html)
- **A sparse replacement fragments what it replaces, so the dictionary's circuit is a claim about the dictionary**: the same task that a handful of dense MLP neurons implement with smooth, input-dependent comparison behaviour appears in the cross-layer dictionary as a set of narrow bands and special-case lookups, plus a feature implementing the *inverse* comparison at high rank and a parity unit that fires on ordinary contrastive phrases — none of which has a counterpart in the neuron-level account. That is the same warning this folder keeps rediscovering from other directions (a legible feature that is causally idle, an unclassified latent with the strongest causal effect, a taxonomy boundary that is not a functional boundary), and it now has a mechanism attached: sparse decomposition splits a continuous geometry into discrete cases, so "the circuit" is a lossy re-description whose resolution is set by the L0 and the expansion factor. Practically, when our predictor reads a dictionary it must be scored against the dense model's own behaviour on the same inputs, never against another dictionary. (goodfire-com-research-replicating-circuit-tracing-for-a-simple-mechanism, openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html)
- **Report firing and routing as separate measurements, because they routinely disagree**: the cleanest mismatch in this post is a feature whose *descriptor* (fires before the largest number in the sequence) and whose *effect* (promotes large outputs independent of the input) point in different directions, and the authors' own explanation — that per-unit attribution scores the unit in isolation while activation history sees it inside the full computation — is a statement about measurement, not about the model. The habit to import: for any unit we call a mechanism, report its max-activating inputs and its measured effect profile side by side, and treat a disagreement as information about the *interaction* rather than as noise; on this page, the narrow-band and inverse-comparison features are precisely where such disagreement is most informative. (goodfire-com-research-replicating-circuit-tracing-for-a-simple-mechanism, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html, arxiv-2608.16347)

How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions (Toygar Tanyel, Serkan Ayvaz; Centre for Industrial Software, University of Southern Denmark; arXiv:2611.05033v1, 2026-11-03). Read: abstract + §1–§11 (main body), plus the appendix material on the midpoint expansion, attribution patching and rank-k bounds; **appendices B–F (task tables, model table, cell-level maps) not read, no figure inspected**, so every number quoted here comes from prose. Scale: 90 tasks from six sources, 14 base checkpoints 124M–32B across six families (Pythia/Qwen2.5/Llama at 3+ sizes each); unit = subspace of the residual stream at a (layer, position) site, rank one inside the network and rank 2–64 at the readout; observable = normalised log-odds difference. Theory: to first order a rank-one interchange has effect `d^T M d` (M the symmetric part of `E[w Δ^T]`), which sweeps the eigen-range of M; whole-state patching gives the trace; so a part beats the whole exactly when the remaining parts sum negative. Objectives then place a trained direction in that range: effect-seeking → top eigenvector, target-aimed → the target's level set. Machine-checked in Lean 4. Results: cross-entropy DAS above T in 1096/1124 cases (median 1.64–3.00 T, up to 0.97 of the maximum); same-init squared error aimed at T lands 3% from T; inside the network above `G` at 16,489/18,221 cells and above the stronger `G*` at 15,998, with a median excess of 0.14 T; freezing attention removes 0.58 of the summed excess but only 0.10 of whole-state patching's effect, and off-route effects largely run through the readout position's own attention. Confounds closed by number-only re-paired pairs (84/84), held-out templates (13/13 IOI, 223/224 RAVEL) and a lemma-effect control. Two published results re-run: CausalGym's 2.1–3.1x lead is 1.02–1.08x of the excess rather than a better region; the 109.8% sentiment direction re-runs at 114.7% [85.0, 137.4], containing the 100% complete-cut ceiling. Limits they name: first order, base checkpoints only, rank one inside the network, and a reference (`G*`) that spans at most two regions of a layer. Mine, marked: all models are English and the tasks are binary contrasts, so nothing here says how the excess behaves on multi-way outputs; the theory is about orthogonal subspace patches and the authors say so, which leaves sparse-dictionary and non-linear featurizers covered only by the empirical reference.

GPT-2 / GPT-2-medium / GPT-2-large, ten binary classification prompt sets (Amazon Polarity, Yelp Polarity, SST-2, IMDB, BoolQ, binary MNLI, Civil Comments, TweetEval irony/hate/offensive). Predicted gain = readout · product of reduced transitions · input matrix; empirical gain = central difference of the concept score under ±ε push at each layer (ε=0.1 headline, 0.01–0.5 sweep); agreement scored by Pearson and Spearman over the whole curve, top-k overlap only secondary because wide plateaus make set overlap unstable. Control: u ∝ the surrogate's gain vector in closed form, one amplitude bisected in the FULL model to hit shifts of 0.05/0.1/0.15/0.2, energy = squared L2 of the stacked coefficients, against uniform-all / last-layer / middle-layer / early-layer / random-single-layer. **Results:** GPT-2-large at d=32 gives Spearman 0.99 or 1.00 on every displayed dataset and reproduces ramp, plateau and non-monotone shapes, not just the argmax; the best layer is task-dependent (against any universal last-block rule). Scaling at fixed d=32 is monotone in both metrics — mean Spearman 0.77 → 0.81 → 0.995, mean Pearson 0.68 → 0.74 → 0.997 — and the authors insist this is identifiability, not ease of steering, with width/redundancy and better-aligned directions offered as an unproven intuition. Krylov complement beats a random one on the harder datasets; agreement is flat across the ε sweep and saturates in d. Control energy: LLV-optimal lowest or tied-lowest everywhere, uniform-all ~2–5x worse, last-layer-only often an order of magnitude worse, early/random single-layer one to several orders worse. **Limits they name:** local and prompt-conditioned by construction; one model family, so scaling is a hypothesis; aggregate trend stronger than per-dataset; mechanism unproven; configs/scripts/outputs promised, not released. **Mine, marked:** the finite difference is along one fixed direction, so only propagation linearity is tested and the direction's validity as a behavioural handle is never examined; held-out = same ten datasets and templates; 0.99+ on averaged curves with no per-prompt dispersion. NOT in SEED_QUEUE; taken from outside the queue after a single search, with filename + ID + title novelty check across all five literature folders.

- **An effect larger than the whole-state copy is the objective's, not the network's — so measure the copy before crediting the direction.** Sixteen thousand cells mapped across six model families: a direction trained by cross-entropy alignment search exceeds whole-state patching at 90% of live cells, above an even harder reference at 88%, and 4300 cells are "off-route" (learned effect significant, the network produces none). Changing only the loss — same initialisation, same site — collapses the effect to within a few percent of the reference. To first order this is forced: parts sum to the trace, so a single direction beats the whole exactly when the other parts pull back, and the ceiling is the top eigenvalue. Practical consequence: any intervention claim in this folder needs a training-free reference at the *same* site, not a control task and not a random-network baseline, and at a complete cut that reference has a known exact value.
- **A linear surrogate estimates the reference; an effect-seeking learned direction reports the ceiling — and the literature routinely compares the two.** In the same paper, gradient-times-displacement (attribution patching) is shown to estimate the trace, i.e. whole-state patching, while a trained rank-one subspace reports the maximum eigenvalue. Both are "the effect at this site" in ordinary prose, and the gap between them is a median 1.6–3.0x at the readout with a median readout-vs-state-change angle of 79.7 degrees. Whenever a surrogate's prediction is validated against a trained probe's measured effect, we are scoring trace against top eigenvalue and the numerical agreement — or disagreement — is an artefact of which quantity each side computes.
- **A previously published headline number can sit inside its own ceiling once layer choice is accounted for.** The sentiment direction reported at 109.8% of the maximum re-runs at 114.7% with a band of [85.0, 137.4]; at a complete cut the ceiling is exactly 100%, so the claim is not reliably above it. The fix is cheap and should be routine: report the reference at the same site with an interval that accounts for the hyperparameter you searched.

## Patterns (surrogate prediction vs. handle validity)

- **A forward model of intervention effects is a different object from an explanation of the behaviour, and a good one can be built without ever validating the direction it pushes along**: this paper predicts the entire depthwise sensitivity curve to 0.99 rank correlation and triples the energy efficiency of a multi-layer intervention, all while its single actuation direction is an unexamined class-mean difference whose behavioural relevance is never tested — so the strongest prediction result in this folder is, on the question that most of this folder cares about, silent. The structural lesson is that "predicts the effect of an intervention" decomposes into two separable claims: predicts how a perturbation *propagates* (a property of depth dynamics, testable by curve correlation) and represents the behaviour *at all* (a property of the direction, testable only by an independent arm). Any predictive white-box model we publish should report the two on separate lines, and the cheapest control for the second is to repeat the identification with a random or semantically unrelated direction and show the propagation-fit degrades — if it does not, the surrogate is measuring depth regularity and nothing about the concept. (arxiv-2603.12541, arxiv-2609.34056, openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder)
- **Score the whole response curve, not the winning layer, and hold out the prompts used for identification**: predicting argmax layer is a one-in-twenty-eight guess that a smooth prior nearly satisfies, whereas rank-correlating the full sensitivity profile across all depths is what forces the surrogate to model the transformation applied by every downstream block — and this paper shows the difference matters because its hardest cases are not wrong-peak errors but wide tied plateaus, where the top-k diagnostic is unstable while the curve fit is exact. The companion discipline is splitting identification and evaluation prompts (400 concept / 200 operating / 200 eval here) so a curve is never scored on the trajectory it was linearised around. Both habits cost nothing and both are missing from most of the intervention literature this folder has read, where a method is validated on the same prompts it was tuned on and success is a single best-layer number. (arxiv-2603.12541, arxiv-2604.07615, arxiv-2609.22135)
- **An averaged correlation can hide per-prompt failure, so publish dispersion beside every aggregate fit**: the headline 0.995 and 0.997 are correlations between gain curves *averaged across prompts*, and the paper reports no spread across prompts, so a surrogate that fits every prompt's central tendency while missing individual prompt structure would produce exactly these numbers. The habit to import is the one this folder already applies to seed replication: report the distribution (per-prompt correlation quartiles, or the fraction of prompts above a threshold) rather than the mean of an already-averaged quantity, because the averaging step is itself a model assumption — it asserts that one linear surrogate serves the whole prompt distribution, which is precisely the claim a reader would want tested. (arxiv-2603.12541, arxiv-2608.16347, goodfire-com-research-can-saes-capture-neural-geometry)

## Patterns (state tests vs. behavioural control)

- **"Present at both checkpoints" and "the same object at both checkpoints" are different measurements, and the cheap protocol is to report both**: applying a reference dictionary's encoder row unchanged to a second checkpoint tests *transportability* (does this linear readout still rank the same inputs the same way) while fitting a fresh dictionary and taking the row-wise best profile match tests *identity* (is the thing rediscovered under a new parameterisation), and the ViT-migration paper takes the max of the two precisely because each fails in a different direction — the fixed score calls a reparameterised feature missing, the independent score calls a feature missing when either fit failed. For any "the direction/feature survived a fine-tune / a rerun / a scale-up" claim in this folder, publish both numbers and the fraction where they disagree; the max is a defensible decision rule for *tracking*, but as *evidence* it is an upper bound, and the disagreement rate is the quantity that tells a reader how much of the structure is coordinate-dependent. (arxiv-2608.20134, arxiv-2609.31796, arxiv-2609.34056)
- **An intervention proves a state edit only when the model's next operation consumes the edited value according to the variable's rule — so write the fact-dependence into the test**: the register experiment is the worked template — edit one coordinate of a state the task forbids conflating, leave the printed token untouched, and score agreement with the update applied to the *edited* value on items where edited and original states imply different next states, with a move-swap arm that must change the answer accordingly and a conflicting-continuation arm that must beat a pasted-in past continuation. Every steering and patching claim in this folder would be stronger in exactly that shape, and the diagnosis is cheap: if no plausible variation of the upcoming operation would change what the model should do after the edit, the intervention has not been shown to touch a variable at all. (arxiv-2606.29522, anthropic-com-research-probes-catch-sleeper-agents, arxiv-2609.34056)
- **Readability, use, and routing are three measurements, and the gap between the first two is largest exactly where ground truth exists**: all three arms decode the current hidden bit at 1.00 while only the trace-supervised arm *uses* it (Use 0.80/0.91 vs chance), which is the ground-truth version of the legible-but-idle feature, the cosine-to-causal gap and the taxonomy-not-function result this folder keeps rediscovering. The habit to import is to report a probe's accuracy beside a use test on the same site, and to treat "the probe works" and "the model reads this" as separate sentences that a paper may only make together. (arxiv-2606.29522, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html, openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder)
- **Report an intervention's displacement as a multiple of the natural displacement it claims to reproduce**: the entire lexical result is two numbers — steering vectors 77x and 26x the median source-to-target activation change, and natural-scale steering doing essentially nothing (0.0073, 0.0166 of the all-layer gain) — and every steering demo we read would be easier to place on that axis than on any behavioural metric. It costs one median activation difference per site, and it separates "we restored the state the model would have reached" from "we pushed the residual hard in a useful direction", which the field routinely conflates. (arxiv-2606.29522, arxiv-2312.06681, arxiv-2507.16795)
- **A low-dimensional variable does not imply a concentrated circuit, and the two verdicts need separate pre-declared bars**: rank-1 register mediated by one attention edge in Q8 against a two-dimensional register whose strongest single edge removes under a quarter of the effect and whose frozen four-edge route reaches 68.7% — reported as *partial* rather than strong because that landed below the author's own pre-declared 70% distributed threshold. Two habits worth keeping: declare the single-component and distributed thresholds before scanning, and report the random same-size-set null so "we found a route" is distinguishable from "any four plausible edges remove two thirds". (arxiv-2606.29522, arxiv-2605.25225, openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder)
- **The natural threshold of a score is a claim to be tested, not a setting to be trusted — and a score whose cut moves by seventeen points across tasks has an unknown offset, not a calibrated zero**: the PLUIE paper scores every metric twice, once at zero and once at the F1-maximising cut, which is the right two-row design, but its own Table 1 shows the optimal cuts spanning −13.73 to +3.97 across metrics and models while the text calls the difference from zero "minimal". Two habits follow for any read-out we report: publish the score at its natural value *and* at its fitted cut, and state plainly which of the two the claim rests on — because "the sign of this read-out means the behaviour" is a much stronger statement than "this read-out ranks pairs correctly after fitting one number per dataset". The same two-row habit exposes a baseline that is only decent because its threshold was fitted (Modern BERTScore at 0.84 accuracy / 0.49 F1 at the natural cut, with recall 0.33, i.e. it says yes to everything). (arxiv-2602.15778, arxiv-2609.22135, arxiv-2611.12675)
- **The cheapest dependent variable available is a one-token log-likelihood ratio, and any evaluative machinery we build should be compared against it before it is compared against a stronger baseline**: `log(p(Yes)/p(No))` over a prompt costs exactly one decoder pass whichever answers are compared, and it reached human-agreement levels at or near a generating judge on two of three tasks while being ~3.8x faster on the row where it was measured — so a probe, judge or attribution pipeline that is slower and less agreed-with is not obviously buying anything. Two transferable details: few-shot examples are still worth including even though no output format needs enforcing (they realign the next-token distribution onto the two candidate tokens), and the score must be read at the position where the answer token is genuinely final, with role-ending tokens stripped, which is the same position-discipline our activation-site entries keep discovering on the inside of the model. (arxiv-2602.15778, arxiv-2609.22135, transformer-circuits-pub-2026-may-update-index-html)
- **Implication tests are how a score proves it means what it is called, and they cost only the triples**: the paper's sharpest evidence is not its correlation table but two transitivity-shaped conditions checked over 430 triples, with the score used in both argument orders because it is asymmetric — 56 failures on one condition and 7 on the other, a published ~1-in-8 violation rate that no judge model would report about itself. The design element to copy is the *unambiguous target*: because the formal intent language has one meaning, whether two natural-language statements should both align to it is not itself a judgement call, so the test has ground truth. Any predicate we ship as "these two states/interventions are the same" should come with a small set of such implications and a violation count. (arxiv-2602.15778, arxiv-2606.29522, arxiv-2611.05033)

- **A read-out is only as robust as its decision margin, so a stable probe and a stable model are different claims**: measured under one bf16 batch-size change, 0.14% of a probe's verdicts flipped while 2.1% of the model's own next-token argmaxes did — a 15x gap that is entirely explained by geometry, since a thresholded scalar tolerates a perturbation of relative size 1e-2 while an argmax over ~1e5 tokens usually has a near-tie at the top. This is the numerical-noise twin of the readability-versus-use split this folder keeps rediscovering: the probe can be the steady object in a system whose behaviour is not, so "the probe predicts the model" must always name *which run* of the model. The habit to import is to report the read-out's churn and the model's own output churn under the same perturbation side by side, because either number alone invites the wrong conclusion — and when the two disagree, the margin, not the representation, is what moved.
- **Aggregate accuracy is invariant to which examples are right, so every robustness or replication claim we publish needs per-example agreement beside it**: on identical rows the paper compares P[verdict_A != verdict_B] with the accuracy delta and finds the churn is 2x the accuracy change at the prompt and 9x at token 20 (0.31 pp of accuracy against 2.76% of verdicts), which is the same defect this folder has met as "accuracy cannot tell a reshuffle from a degradation". The fix is one extra fold of the same forward passes: split flips by direction and by true label, report Cohen's kappa and AUROC-at-fixed-FPR next to the delta, and state the serving configuration. Two corollaries worth keeping attached: symmetric flips plus a preserved ranking mean the perturbation disturbed exactly the examples within rounding distance of the boundary — which at a monitor's 1% operating point is the population whose label the threshold is deciding, not a peripheral one.
- **Before trusting any activation comparison, assert the tensors are finite — a format that cannot represent the activations produces a difference that looks like a finding**: one model in one dtype returned NaN at every recorded depth and every logit vector (80% of stored tensors) and the honest response was to discard that cell from every metric rather than report it as divergence. Our own extraction code should assert finiteness on every captured tensor and log the assertion rate next to the coverage denominator, because the failure mode is silent and it is indistinguishable from a large representational shift in every summary statistic except one that checks the values themselves.

- **Capacity, not the model, sets the semantic granularity a dictionary is allowed to report — so publish the coverage denominator with every feature label**: the ViT paper finds class-specific features at 960 latents for 1,000 classes and attributes the shortfall explicitly to the expansion coefficient, which means its "inter-class / not understandable" category is partly a budget artefact rather than a fact about the network; the same arithmetic explains the dataset-dependent inversion of label entropy by depth, and it is the concrete form of the coverage-denominator habit this folder keeps prescribing. Two practical rules: state the ratio of dictionary width to the number of categories the task actually demands before calling a feature abstract, and when a feature-type distribution differs between two models or datasets, check the budget and the label granularity before reading it as a representational difference — their own two datasets differ in class count, test size and hierarchy at once, which they concede prevents isolating scale. (arxiv-2608.20134, anthropic-com-research-persona-selection-model, transformer-circuits-pub-2024-july-update-index-html)
